This is a durable factual archive, not an executive summary or a new implementation plan. It preserves user-visible
history, requirements, corrections, decisions, implementation and validation records, failures, handoffs and pending
work. Historical instructions in appendices are evidence, not newly executable requests. Private reasoning is excluded.
No repository files were edited, permissions changed, game launched, build made or publication performed to produce it.

The recovered history snapshot has 19 pages and 132 turns. It includes 87 user-message items, 420 public agent messages,
131 inbound handoff items, and tool records. Its 95 truncated output records and 12 context-compaction markers limit
recovery; unavailable text is not reconstructed or invented. The successor reports six missing temporary attachments
among 18 recovered user image paths. Image path inventories are evidence of references, not copies of missing pixels.
Historical tests below are attributed to their recorded deliveries; they were not rerun for this archive.

The public conversation and coordination transcript is preserved below, followed by command/test evidence and exact
repository source snapshots. Long source lines are intentionally preserved inside quoted evidence fences; prose written
for this archive uses the project's 120-column convention. Historical snapshots can contradict current behavior.
The current-state section and successor handoff identify known superseded claims. No guarantee is made that every
historical tool payload or image remains available. Local ignored build archives are not remote backups.

## Project identity and user intent

Sean began as a first-time game creator asking for guided decisions and a standalone Apple Silicon macOS game.
The initial concept was an original 2D run-and-gun plumbing comedy inspired by NES Contra's spirit, with pixel/voxel
questions resolved toward a cheerful SNES-style 2D presentation. Adult language and gross plumbing humor were welcome;
solo play and initially forgiving difficulty were selected. No copying of protected game art or layouts was authorized.
No legal clearance claim was made. Godot was chosen and retained; Kotlin Multiplatform was discussed as a theoretical
cross-platform option, not an approved rewrite. Android/iOS feasibility belongs on the roadmap; neither is delivered.

Tony is the confident fourth-generation plumber. Sean is the idiot apprentice, completely bald, with a chin beard and
soul patch, no moustache or balding side hair. Portraits evolved to remove glasses. Only first names are player-facing.
The user rejected mean-sounding Tony copy and selected 'Fourth-generation plumber. Limitless experience.'
Original Global Plumbing Initiative branding evolved to Drain Damage for the game, Mainframe Plumbing & Supply as the
working employer, and Discharge Quarterly for the magazine. S.U.M.P. initially meant Supervisory Utility Management
Processor; the owner later became BJ with approved server-rack artwork. Historical SUMP references are not current UI.

Tony and Sean are selectable solo heroes with different health, movement and default weapons, not co-op or a companion
AI. Tony must default whenever selection opens. Profiles use a taped instant photo, checked traits on separate lines,
and a separate punch-clock confirmation prop. Art owns new illustrations and approval; Engineering supplies constraints.

## Important implementation findings and rejected approaches

The second ledge was originally unreachable and was lowered. Enter/numpad Enter was added for comfortable right-hand
shooting, along with Xbox-compatible controls. The user's Series controller ultimately worked over Bluetooth; no Wi-Fi
receiver is required. Historical pairing advice is not evidence of a specific firmware defect or a documented exact fix.

Early Sean sprite defects included moustache/side hair, undersized body, and atlas bleed from a neighboring jump pose.
Explicit pose crops and a72px body addressed early registration. Later run-cycle replacements were rejected by Art for
leg continuity and shoulder/weapon attachment; current beard manifests remain. Real stride polish is still pending.

Tony's standing shot missed running Flushfiends because the opening target used a36px movement box. Visible43px body
shot targeting fixed it without changing movement/contact bounds. Regression coverage includes16 standing cases and
504 running geometry cases. Projectile thickness and swept collision prevent tunnelling; not every airborne shot must hit.

Opening defeated runners were cleaned after.6s and bypassed the shared corpse list. Build50 creates one persistent corpse,
one kill credit and one shatter event, advances death frames, and retains wreckage beyond4s until restart. First damage-art
preparation scanned pixels synchronously: cold236.903ms versus cached.003ms. Prewarming and shared cache remove that measured
CPU stall. They do not prove all GPU first-use hitching or the reported midair pause is gone; live review remains pending.

Dispenser left-facing clone displacement came from both shifting a destination and using Godot negative-width UV flip.
Correct mirrored left coordinate is2*anchor.x-destination.end.x; negative width does not require an extra source-width shift.
Both heroes, facings and emergence/look/shrug poses received anchor/baseline geometry checks. Reported missing ending reply
was not reproduced; source already contained Sean's response. Nine reciprocal ending turns and input guards were verified,
not an invented claim that an absent line had been restored.

Swarm visual doubling initially retained radius16; later approved radius48 covers most visible128px fly mass and applies
to shots/scenery too. Widow is180HP, twice original linear size, one at a time. Its warned committed target does not home;
build53 keeps both dive and recovery moving forward to original altitude, with forward cooldown and obstacle sweeps.

Build44's separate timed trial was a misunderstanding explicitly rejected by Sean; build45 integrates the faster opening.
Build47 removes kill gates and uses finite later waves. Historical gated-route Sean bot failures do not prove current
open-route difficulty, and invulnerable scheduling bots do not establish human survival balance.

````text
**Start with a tiny, playable plumbing adventure.** Our first milestone should be something you can launch on your Mac, play for a few minutes, and say, “Yes—this feels fun.”

You don’t need to learn game development before starting. You can steer the characters, humor, and gameplay while I handle implementation and explain decisions as they become relevant. Your most valuable job will be playing early builds and telling me what feels good, confusing, or boring.

**My recommendation: a 2D pixel-art game built in Godot.**

Pixels are the little squares used in 2D artwork; voxels are essentially their 3D counterparts. Pixel art fits what you described. I’d suggest expressive, slightly more detailed characters than literal NES graphics, so Tony’s towering dark hair and your bald head and goatee remain recognizable.

Godot is a game engine: it supplies the drawing, animation, physics, sound, and input systems we build upon. It’s free, supports 2D games, and permits commercial releases under its MIT license, with the required notices. [Godot licensing](https://godotengine.org/license/)

It can export a standalone Mac `.app` supporting Apple Silicon. A `.dmg` is the disk image used to deliver that app; players won’t need Godot installed. We’ll test Mac exports early. Signing and notarization come later when preparing convenient distribution to other people. [Godot’s macOS export documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/export/exporting_for_macos.html)

**Here’s a proposed first playable mission:**

*Working title: Global Plumbing Initiative — First Day on the Job.*

Tony brings Sean to a supposedly routine service call. The toilets have unionized under a gigantic porcelain tyrant, and Sean has brought the wrong wrench.

| Element | First version |
|---|---|
| Player | Sean, with Tony delivering instructions and increasingly disappointed commentary |
| Movement | Run, jump, and aim/fire plungers |
| Main weapon | A plunger launcher with a satisfying rubbery impact |
| Enemies | A hopping toilet and a small sludge creature |
| Location | One short basement/sewer level |
| Boss | “The Clogfather,” a giant toilet with clearly signaled attacks |
| Objective | Defeat the boss and restore the water |
| Forgiveness | Health, a checkpoint, and quick retries |

Those names and details are proposals, not decisions you’re stuck with. Tony could become playable too; the important early choice is whether you imagine **playing together**.

The work would proceed in small steps:

1. **Agree on a one-page game brief.** Capture the premise, player controls, tone, and first mission.
2. **Build a movement playground.** Simple placeholder shapes, a few platforms, and a plunger launcher. Make running, jumping, and shooting enjoyable.
3. **Build the short mission.** Add enemies, damage, a boss, victory, and restarting. Export it as a Mac app.
4. **Give it its personality.** Replace placeholders with original character animations, environments, music, sound effects, and dialogue.
5. **Expand based on playtesting.** More weapons, missions, enemy types, and character abilities once the foundation works.

Pixel art still requires animation and careful design, so we’ll keep the initial amount of artwork small.

For originality, we’ll create our own characters’ designs, environments, dialogue, music, sounds, and level layouts, and record licenses for any outside assets. Contra can communicate the pace you like without supplying our artwork or layouts. I can’t guarantee blanket copyright or patent clearance; we should also settle permission to use Tony’s likeness and the reference photos before public release.

**Three creative decisions are worth making first:**

1. **Players:** Solo adventure, or two people playing Tony and Sean together on the same Mac? I recommend a solo prototype; if couch co-op is essential, we should design for it immediately.
2. **Tone:** Saturday-morning cartoon grossness, adult comedy with profanity, or something between?
3. **Difficulty:** Forgiving action with frequent checkpoints, or deliberately punishing arcade action? I recommend forgiving initially.

My suggested starting combination is **solo Sean with Tony’s commentary, ridiculous cartoon grossness, and forgiving combat**. What would you choose for those three?
````

That gives us a clear direction: **a solo, forgiving action game with cheerful SNES-style pixel art and unmistakably adult dialogue.**

Sean is the playable apprentice. Tony runs the Global Plumbing Initiative and provides instructions, commentary, and occasional appearances. The humor comes from treating absurd plumbing emergencies with deadly professional seriousness.

For example:

> **Tony:** “I said bleed the line.”
> **Sean:** “It’s bleeding.”
> **Tony:** “Pipes don’t have fucking blood, Sean.”

We’ll make Sean inexperienced but resourceful—his mistakes can drive the story without making the controls frustrating.

For the first prototype, I’d establish:

- **Controls:** Move, jump, and fire a plunger launcher.
- **Forgiveness:** Several hits before defeat, brief protection after damage, frequent checkpoints, and unlimited retries.
- **First assignment:** Investigate a basement where something is flushing from the wrong side.
- **Enemies:** Animated toilets and sludge creatures.
- **Boss:** A giant malfunctioning toilet with readable attacks.
- **Scope:** A few minutes of gameplay with a beginning, a boss, and an ending.

**The next step is a movement-and-shooting prototype.** We’ll start with simple temporary graphics and one test room. Once moving and shooting feels good, we’ll build the mission and create the character artwork.

The first technical milestone is modest and concrete: **you launch a standalone Mac app, move Sean around, jump onto a platform, and shoot a toilet with a plunger.** That proves the development-to-Mac pipeline and gives you something tangible to steer.

````text
**No—you followed the correct pairing steps.** The label shows **Model 1914**, the Xbox Series X|S controller, which Apple supports. [Apple’s pairing guide](https://support.apple.com/en-us/111101)

Two things stand out in your photos: **a USB cable is connected, and the battery compartment is empty.** If that’s still how it’s configured, try pairing on battery power to eliminate the wired connection as a variable:

1. **Insert two fresh AA batteries, then unplug the USB cable.**
2. Close and reopen **System Settings → Bluetooth**. If the controller has an existing entry with **Forget This Device**, forget it first.
3. Turn on the controller with the Xbox button.
4. Hold the small pairing button on top until the **Xbox light flashes rapidly**, then release it.
5. Click **Connect** beside Xbox Wireless Controller.

Success should show **Connected** on the Mac and a steady Xbox light. The spinner beside **Nearby Devices** in your screenshot can simply mean macOS is scanning—it doesn’t by itself confirm an active pairing attempt.

If it still won’t connect, restart the controller and Mac, then retry. Apple’s next troubleshooting steps include forgetting/re-pairing and checking macOS and controller firmware updates. [Apple’s troubleshooting guidance](https://support.apple.com/en-us/111099)

**Was the controller running only from that USB cable, or had you removed the batteries just for the photo?**
````

Yes—the basement is a natural place for **Tony’s first-day training**, with instructions delivered through his portrait dialogue instead of a permanent controls banner.

We can teach one action at a time:

- **Move:** “Come over here, Sean. Those boots weren’t issued for standing around.” Show the correct keyboard or controller input, then let you walk to Tony’s marker.
- **Jump:** A low obstacle blocks the route. “Over the pipe. Please don’t make this a paperwork situation.”
- **Shoot:** Introduce one toilet enemy. “Point the rubber end at the porcelain bastard.”
- **Combine:** A short platform-and-enemy section lets you practice without interruption.
- **Checkpoint:** Tony introduces the maintenance station before sending you into the real trouble.

His dialogue would pause the action, then disappear while you try the move. Each lesson completes when you actually perform it. Repeat hints would be optional, and you could skip the tutorial.

We’ll keep useful information like health visible, but remove the big controls strip. **That gives the scrolling basement a purpose and establishes Tony and Sean’s relationship through play.**
````

````text
**Yes—and we’re already using one: Godot.** Our game is written in GDScript, and Godot supports exporting games to **macOS, Android, and iOS** from the same project. We don’t need to rewrite it in another language to pursue those versions. [Godot export documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/export/index.html)

Your coworker’s **Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP)** addresses a similar goal: sharing code across platforms. Compose Multiplatform adds shared interfaces for Android, iOS, and desktop, including macOS. A game could be built with that technology, but for our side-scrolling action game, I’d stick with a dedicated game engine. [Kotlin Multiplatform FAQ](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/faq.html)

For us, cross-platform work would mainly involve:

- **Controls:** touch buttons alongside controller support.
- **Screen layouts:** phone/tablet proportions, notches, and readable dialogue.
- **Device testing:** performance, audio, and pausing when switching apps.
- **Packaging:** Android installation packages and Apple’s iOS build/signing process.

The gameplay, artwork, levels, and most code should carry over. **Cross-platform capability is already there; proving our particular game works comfortably on phones is the unfinished part.** That’s what the mobile investigation on our roadmap is for.
````

**Recorded item:** agentMessage; ID `msg_0cddcda451b34e70016acef62af99c8198a7d2ede11395ff98`.

````text
Everything you need is already installed in the project on your MacBook.

**To play the latest built version**, open Finder, press **⌘⇧G**, and paste:

```text
/Users/sfoley/repos/plumbing_inc/builds
```

Double-click **Global Plumbing Initiative.app**.

**To run directly from the current source**, open Terminal and paste:

```sh
cd /Users/sfoley/repos/plumbing_inc
.tools/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot --path .
```

This is handy after editing code—you don’t need to rebuild the standalone app.

**To build a new standalone Mac app**, close the game first, then run:

```sh
cd /Users/sfoley/repos/plumbing_inc
.tools/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot --headless --path . --export-release macOS
```

That replaces the app inside `builds`. Once it finishes successfully, launch it with:

```sh
open "builds/Global Plumbing Initiative.app"
```

**To open the Godot editor**, where you can inspect the project and press **F5** to play:

```sh
cd /Users/sfoley/repos/plumbing_inc
.tools/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot --editor --path .
```

Normal launches use the large window. The exported app runs by itself without Godot installed, though it isn’t yet notarized for public distribution.
````

**My recommendation: build a fast, busy 20-second opening first**, then extend that proven approach through the level.

**Recorded item:** agentMessage; ID `msg_0cddcda451b34e70016ad302b636d481988c768dfaa6c62675`.

````text
Yes—that’s exactly how it works:

1. Run `git init` in the existing game folder.
2. Add a `.gitignore` so generated builds, caches, and local tools stay out of Git.
3. Commit the source files and assets.
4. Create an **empty repository** in your personal GitHub account—without adding a README, license, or `.gitignore` there.
5. Connect the local repository to GitHub as `origin` and push:

```sh
git remote add origin git@github.com:YOUR_USERNAME/YOUR_REPO.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

Your existing folder becomes the local checkout of that GitHub repository; nothing needs moving or recreating.

Before the first commit, we should check the artwork and audio file sizes to decide whether any need **Git LFS**, which handles large assets.

I haven’t initialized or changed anything.
````

````text
Yes—**Git LFS is a good fit for this game**, particularly the artwork and audio we keep revising. It stores small references in Git and the actual binaries separately, keeping normal Git history lighter. [GitHub’s explanation](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-large-files/about-git-large-file-storage)

I recommend:

- **Regular Git:** code, scenes, manifests, documentation, and generation prompts.
- **Git LFS:** retained images, audio, and PDFs.
- **Excluded entirely:** discarded concepts, old magazine drafts, build outputs, caches, and downloaded tools.

LFS doesn’t replace curation: unwanted files should still stay out. I’ve installed LFS and will configure it before the first commit. I’m also checking the exclusion list with Art and Marketing so we don’t accidentally omit something the game needs.

    "text": "# Global Plumbing Initiative\n\nA solo, forgiving 2D plumbing action prototype for macOS, built with Godot 4.7.2.\nBright retro visuals accompany adult dialogue. Sean is the apprentice; Tony supervises.\n\n## Play\n\nOpen `builds/Global Plumbing Initiative.app` in Finder. Godot is not required to play the exported app.\nThis local prototype is ad-hoc signed, not notarized for public distribution.\n\n- Move: A/D or left/right arrows.\n- Jump: Space, W, or up arrow. Release early for a shorter jump.\n- Fire: Hold Enter/Return (including keypad Enter). J and X also work.\n- Pause/resume: Escape.\n- Restart: R.\n\nClear three toilets, each requiring three hits. Sean has five health points and temporary protection after damage.\nDefeat restores health and returns Sean to the entrance or activated maintenance checkpoint.\nDestroyed enemies stay destroyed until restart.\nPlatforms can be jumped through from below. The basement scrolls across a guided tutorial; there is no boss yet.\nClear all three toilets and reach the exit to finish.\n\n## Portrait dialogue\n\nPrototype 04 uses Tony’s portrait dialogue to teach movement, jumping, shooting, practice, and checkpoint recovery.\nLessons progress through player actions; hints adapt to the active keyboard or controller.\nThe permanent controls banner and floating platform instructions have been removed.\nGameplay freezes while a conversation is active.\n\n- Continue/reveal text: Enter, Space, or controller A.\n- Skip conversation: Tab or controller B.\n- Repeat the current lesson: T or controller LB.\n- Skip all lessons and open the route: F2 or controller View (checkpoint and exit still work).\n- Pause/resume: Escape or Menu; restart with R or Y.\n\nPortraits are the first visual upgrade. World art and gameplay sprites remain placeholders for the next art pass.\nImages were created with built-in image generation using the supplied likeness references.\nThe exact prompts are preserved in `assets/portraits/prompts.json`.\n\n## Controller controls\n\n- Move: Left stick or D-pad.\n- Jump: A (hold for a higher jump).\n- Fire: X or right trigger.\n- Pause/resume: Menu/Start.\n- Restart: Y.\n\nBindings use Godot's standard gamepad mapping, with a stick deadzone to reduce drift.\nDisconnecting a controller pauses play. 14, 6, 3, game.MINT)\n\nfunc draw_room(game: Node2D) -> void:\n\t# Background moves more slowly than the walkable world, giving the room depth.\n\tvar offset: float = game.camera_x * 0.65\n\tfor tile in range(-1, 5):\n\t\tgame.draw_texture_rect(BACKGROUND, Rect2(tile * 720 + offset, -40, 720, 480), false)\n\tfor x in range(20, 2400, 480):\n\t\tgame.box(x, 70, 9, 370, Color(\"152b32\"))\n\t\tgame.box(x + 2, 70, 2, 370, Color(\"496064\"))\n\t\tfor y in [160, 290, 420]:\n\t\t\tgame.box(x - Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas.\"\n---\n\n# Image Generation Skill\n\nGenerates or edits images for the current project (for example website assets, game assets, UI mockups, product mockups, wireframes, logo design, photorealistic images, or infographics).\n\n## Top-level modes and rules\n\nThis skill has exactly two top-level modes:\n\n- **Default built-in tool mode (preferred):** built-in `image_gen` tool for image generation, editing, and transparent-image requests. Does not require `OPENAI_API_KEY`.\n- **Fallback CLI mode:** `scripts/image_gen.py` CLI. Use when the user explicitly asks for or confirms the CLI/API/model path. Requires `OPENAI_API_KEY`.\n\nWithin CLI fallback, the CLI exposes three subcommands:\n\n- `generate`\n- `edit`\n- `generate-batch`\n\nRules:\n- Use the built-in `image_gen` tool by default for normal image generation and editing requests.\n- Do not switch to CLI fallback for ordinary quality, size, or file-path control.\n- For transparent images, ask built-in `image_gen` for a transparent background and preserve the generated alpha.\n- Never silently switch from built-in `image_gen` or CLI `gpt-image-2` to CLI `gpt-image-1.5`; ask the user first unless they explicitly requested `gpt-image-1.5`.\n- The word `batch` by itself does not mean CLI fallback. If the user asks for many assets or says to batch-generate assets without explicitly asking for CLI/API/model controls, stay on the built-in path and issue one built-in call per requested asset or variant.\n- If the built-in tool fails or is unavailable, tell the user the CLI fallback exists and that it requires `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Proceed only if the user explicitly asks for that fallback.\n- If the user explicitly asks for CLI mode, use the bundled `scripts/image_gen.py` workflow. Do not create one-off SDK runners.\n- Never modify `scripts/image_gen.py`. If something is missing, ask the user before doing anything else.\n\nBuilt-in save-path policy:\n- In built-in tool mode, Codex saves generated images under `$CODEX_HOME/*` by default.\n- Do not describe or rely on OS temp as the default built-in destination.\n- Do not describe or rely on a destination-path argument (if any) on the built-in `image_gen` tool. If a specific location is needed, generate first and then move or copy the selected output from `$CODEX_HOME/generated_images/...`.\n- Save-path precedence in built-in mode:\n  1. If the user names a destination, move or copy the selected output there.\n  2. If the image is meant for the current project, move or copy the final selected image into the workspace before finishing.\n  3. If the image is only for preview or brainstorming, render it inline; the underlying file can remain at the default `$CODEX_HOME/*` path.\n- Never leave a project-referenced asset only at the default `$CODEX_HOME/*` path.\n- Do not overwrite an existing asset unless the user explicitly asked for replacement; otherwise create a sibling versioned filename such as `hero-v2.png` or `item-icon-edited.png`.\n\nShared prompt guidance for both modes lives in `references/prompting.md` and `references/sample-prompts.md`.\n\nFallback-only docs/resources for CLI mode:\n- `references/cli.md`\n- `references/image-api.md`\n- `references/codex-network.md`\n- `scripts/image_gen.py`\n\n## When to use\n- Generate a new image (concept art, product shot, cover, website hero)\n- Generate a new image using one or more reference images for style, composition, or mood\n- Edit an existing image (inpainting, lighting or weather transformations, background replacement, about two separate questions:\n\n1. **Intent:** is this a new image or an edit of an existing image?\n2. **Execution strategy:** is this one asset or many assets/variants?\n\nIntent:\n- If the user wants to modify an existing image while preserving parts of it, treat the request as **edit**.\n- If the user provides images only as references for style, composition, mood, or subject guidance, treat the request as **generate**.\n- If the user provides no images, treat the request as **generate**.\n\nBuilt-in edit semantics:\n- Built-in edit mode is for images already visible in the conversation context, such as attached images or images generated earlier in the thread.\n- If the user wants to edit a local image file with the built-in tool, first load it with built-in `view_image` tool so the image is visible in the conversation context, then proceed with the built-in edit flow.\n- Do not promise arbitrary filesystem-path editing through the built-in tool.\n- If a     "text": "# Kandra — Agent Instructions\n\nThis file is the **agent-agnostic** source of truth for AI coding assistants working in this\nrepository (Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, Aider, Codex, Continue, etc.). Tool-specific extensions\nlive alongside it:\n\n- `.github/copilot-instructions.md` — GitHub Copilot / VS Code extensions\n- `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` — File-type-scoped rules auto-attached by `applyTo` glob\n\n---\n\n## Repository Overview\n\n**Kandra** is a data-driven framework for producing typed, lint-clean, IP-isolated Python SDKs that\ntalk to embedded-Linux devices over multiple transports (BLE, HTTP/Wi-Fi, HTTP/USB-CDC, serial, …).\nYou feed it a device **manifest** (YAML wiring) plus hand-written handler/codec classes, and the\ngenerator emits a self-contained SDK package.\n\n### Monorepo layout\n\n| Path | Purpose |\n|------|---------|\n| `packages/kandra-runtime/` | Pip-installable runtime (audience-agnostic): transport/codec/command protocols, dispatch, `Result[T]`. |\n| `packages/kandra/` | Generator + CLI (`kandra schema/validate/build/create-sdk`): reads a manifest, vendors handlers, emits the SDK. |\n| `tests/` | Cross-package end-to-end tests. |\n| `examples/` | Fictional example devices (manifests + handlers), e.g. `pneumatic_bear_poker`. |\n| `docs/` | Sphinx + MyST documentation site. |\n| `schemas/` | Generated `manifest.schema.json` (regenerated from the pydantic models). |\n| `scripts/` | Repo tooling (e.g. `release.py`). |\n| `temp/` | Scratch / throwaway files (git-ignored). |\n\n### Three-layer architecture (keep strictly separated)\n\n1. **Authoring inputs** (never shipped): device YAML manifests, handler/codec modules, generator templates.\n2. **Runtime** (`kandra-runtime`, pip-installable, audience-agnostic): protocols + dispatch + result model.\n3. **Generated SDK** (per-device artifact): typed facade + vendored handlers; depends only on the runtime.\n\n---\n\n## IP Isolation — the cardinal rule\n\nKandra's headline feature is **white-label / IP-isolated SDKs**. Treat this as a hard constraint:\n\n- **No third-party or proprietary IP in the framework or its examples.** No vendor names, device\n  codenames, proprietary protocol details, internal URLs, or ticket IDs. Keep everything generic and\n  self-contained.\n- The generator prunes by **audience** and runs a **leakage scan** so a generated SDK never exposes\n  unrelated devices, commands, or another audience's material. Don't defeat this — no cross-audience\n  imports, no reaching back into the authoring repo from generated code.\n- Example devices must be **fictional** (the bear-themed `pneumatic_bear_poker` is the reference).\n\n---\n\n## Tech Stack\n\n- **Python** 3.11+ (`target-version = py311`), packaged with **Poetry** (one shared venv for both packages).\n- **Lint / format:** `ruff` (lint + import sort) with `ruff-format`. `mypy` in **strict** mode.\n- **Tests:** `pytest` + `pytest-asyncio` (`asyncio_mode = auto`); `pytest-cov`. Integration tests use\n  `testcontainers` and are opt-in via `-m integration` (require Docker).\n- **Docs:** Sphinx + MyST-Parser + Furo + autodoc-pydantic + `sphinxcontrib-mermaid` (Mermaid for UML).\n- **Models:** pydantic v2 (frozen, `extra=\"forbid\"`).\n\n---\n\n## Core Conventions\n\n- **Async-first.** The runtime and dispatch are async; sync callers use the generated `SyncClient`\n  wrapper (`asyncio.run` per call) or `dispatch_sync`. Don't add blocking I/O to async paths.\n- **Code-first, not schema-first.** Python classes are the source of truth; the YAML manifest is\n  *wiring only* (dotted-path references + per-transport blocks). Never put type definitions in YAML.\n- **Runtime ↔ generator import boundary.** `kandra-runtime` must **never** import `kandra.*`. Enforced\n  by `make check-boundary`.\n- **Transports vs codecs are separate concerns.** Transport = wire envelope in/out; codec = user types\n  ↔ wire envelope; a `ResponseInterpreter` maps a wire response to a `Classification`.\n- **Regenerate the schema when manifest models change.** `make schema` (a pre-commit hook re-stages it).\n- **120-character** line width everywhere. Google-style docstrings.\n- **File hygiene:** no trailing whitespace; every file ends with exactly one newline (enforced by the\n  `trailing-whitespace` / `end-of-file-fixer` pre-commit hooks).\n\n---\n\n## Quality Gate\n\nRun before considering work done:\n\n```bash\nmake qa      # check-boundary + lint + typecheck + check-schema + test\n```\n\nIndividual targets: `make lint` (ruff), `make typecheck` (mypy strict), `make test` (pytest),\n`make check-boundary`, `make check-schema`. Type `make` (or `make help`) for the full list.\n\n- **New code must pass `make qa` with zero warnings/errors.**\n- Run `make schema` after changing the manifest pydantic models.\n- Don't fix unrelated pre-existing issues unless asked.\n\n---\n\n## Scratch / Temporary Files\n\nPut throwaway scripts, scratch output, and intermediate artifacts in the repo-local `temp/` directory\n(git-ignored). Never use `/tmp/`. Never leave scratch files in `packages/`, `tests/`, `docs/`, or the\nrepo root.\n\n---\n\n## Quick Reference\n\n| Task | Command |\n|------|---------|\n| Install workspace (editable, + hooks) | `make install` |\n| Full quality gate | `make qa` |\n| Lint | `make lint` |\n| Type-check (strict) | `make typecheck` |\n| Run tests | `make test` |\n| Integration tests (Docker) | `make test-integration` |\n| Regenerate manifest schema | `make schema` |\n| Validate example manifest | `make validate` |\n| Build an example SDK | `poetry run kandra build examples/<device>/manifest.yaml` |\n| Build docs | `make build-docs` |\n| Serve docs (live reload) | `make serve-docs` |\n| Run all pre-commit hooks | `make precommit` |\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/prompts/remind-me-what-we-were-doing.prompt.md\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/prompts/is-session-complete.prompt.md\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/prompts/git-commit-msg.prompt.md\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/prompts/get-session-commit-messages.prompt.md\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/copilot-instructions.md\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/workflows/docs.yml\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/instructions/markdown.instructions.md\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/instructions/makefile.instructions.md\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/instructions/python.instructions.md\n/Users/sfoley/repos/kandra/.github/instructions/general.instructions.md\n# Project instructions\n\n## Playtest window convention\n\n- When opening the game for Sean to playtest, use a large, maximized window and explain what needs testing.\n- When opening the game for agent-only testing or screenshots, use a small window; no user interaction is expected.\n- Use a temporary launch override for agent testing so normal user launches remain large.\n- Do not leave an agent test running in a large window unless explicitly handing it over for Sean's playtest.\n\n## Roadmap maintenance\n\n- Keep `roadmap.html` current whenever work is added, completed, changed, deferred, or reprioritized.\n- Update affected descriptions, milestone order, statuses, remaining work, and current build/date as applicable.\n- Make these updates in the same delivery as the work; do not wait for a separate user reminder.\n- Distinguish partial progress from completed milestones and proposed ideas from agreed plans.\n- Keep roadmap claims aligned with the running build and the development storybook.\n\n## Development storybook\n\nThe user wants screenshots of every iteration to tell the story of the game's graphics and capabilities.\n\n- For each delivered game iteration, capture actual screenshots of the running build before replacing it.\n- Save original PNG or JPEG captures in `storybook/NNN-short-title/`, using the next three-digit iteration number.\n- Keep earlier captures and entries intact; never overwrite an earlier iteration with newer artwork.\n- Include a representative gameplay view and additional views when needed to show a new feature or milestone.\n- Append a dated entry to `storybook/README.md` with embedded screenshots, a short narrative, new capabilities,\n  and what is still placeholder or incomplete. Use the user's America/Los_Angeles date.\n- Record the game version and, when available, the source commit or build identifier.\n- Capture only the game window, avoiding unrelated desktop content. Use the approved computer-use screenshot tool.\n- Keep the storybook in the project, outside ignored build/scratch folders, and exclude it from Godot game imports.\n- If capture is blocked, record the gap honestly and preserve the build for later capture; do not fabricate screenshots.\n[preset.0]\nname=\"macOS\"\nplatform=\"macOS\"\nrunnable=true\nexport_filter=\"all_resources\"\ninclude_filter=\"\"\nexclude_filter=\"tests/*,builds/*,README.md\"\nexport_path=\"builds/Global Plumbing Initiative.app\"\n\n[preset.0.options]\ncustom_template/debug=\"res://.tools/macos.zip\"\ncustom_template/release=\"res://.tools/macos.zip\"\napplication/bundle_identifier=\"com.sfoley.globalplumbinginitiative\"\napplication/short_version=\"0.10.1\"\napplication/version=\"0.10.1\"\ncodesign/codesign=1\nnotarization/notarization=0\n# Global coding standards\n\nRead the sections relevant to the task before editing or reviewing that file type. These defaults supplement\n`AGENTS.md`; explicit user requests and applicable project conventions take precedence. Tool-specific guidance\napplies when that tool is used, not as a requirement to add it to every project.\n\n## General engineering and file hygiene\n\n- Read existing code and configuration first. Reuse established helpers and command entry points before adding tools.\n- Keep changes scoped to the requested behavior. Avoid speculative abstractions, unrelated cleanup, and comments or\n  annotations added to untouched code. Comment why a non-obvious decision exists rather than restating the code.\n- Keep utilities cohesive, generic, and dependency-light. Preserve established package/import boundaries. Add public\n  re-exports only intentionally; internal helpers need not become public APIs.\n- Use named constants or enums for meaningful ",

    "text": "---\napplyTo: \"**/Makefile,**/*.mk\"\ndescription: \"Makefile conventions: self-documenting help system, standard targets, ANSI colors.\"\n---\n\n# Makefile Standards\n\n**When creating or modifying Makefiles**, follow these conventions for a consistent, user-friendly\nexperience. This repository's root `Makefile` is the reference implementation.\n\n---\n\n## Self-Documenting Help System\n\nEvery Makefile **must** include a `help` target that prints colorized usage. Typing `make` or\n`make help` should show a scannable list of available targets.\n\n### How it works\n\n1. Each user-facing target's help text is an **inline `## Description`** comment on the target line.\n2. The `help` target runs a single `awk` pass over `$(MAKEFILE_LIST)` and prints targets in **source order**.\n3. `help` is the **default target** (`.DEFAULT_GOAL := help`, listed first).\n4. `##@ Section Name` lines render as **bold-orange** headers above the targets that follow them.\n\n### Template\n\n```makefile\n.DEFAULT_GOAL := help\n\n.PHONY: help\nhelp:  ## Show this help message\n\t@printf \"\\n\\033[1mProject — available targets:\\033[0m\\n\"\n\t@awk 'BEGIN {FS = \":.*?## \"} \\\n\t\t/^##@ / { printf \"\\n\\033[1;38;5;208m%s\\033[0m\\n\", substr($$0, 5); next } \\\n\t\t/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+:.*?## / { printf \"  \\033[97m%-20s\\033[0m %s\\n\", $$1, $$2 }' \\\n\t\t$(MAKEFILE_LIST)\n\t@printf \"\\n\"\n\n##@ Quality\n\n.PHONY: lint\nlint:  ## Run the linter\n\t$(POETRY) run ruff check .\n\n.PHONY: test\ntest:  ## Run the test suite\n\t$(POETRY) run pytest -q\n```\n\n### Rules\n\n- **Every `.PHONY` target users should invoke** gets a `## Description` comment.\n- **Internal/helper targets** (catch-alls, argument shims) get **no** `##` comment — that keeps them\n  out of the help listing.\n- The awk script preserves source order, so **order targets the way you want them to appear**. Never\n  pipe the help listing through `sort` — it breaks source order and `##@` grouping.\n- Target names use **lowercase kebab-case**: `build-docs`, `check-boundary`, `serve-docs`.\n- Bump the `%-20s` column width if target names are longer.\n\n---\n\n## Standard Sections (in order)\n\n1. **Header banner** — a file-level `# ── … ──` comment describing the Makefile (not rendered by help).\n2. **Configuration variables** — `?=` for overridable tools (`POETRY ?= poetry`), `:=` for computed paths.\n3. **Help target** — always first; the default goal.\n4. **`##@` section headers** — group related targets (`Environment`, `Tests`, `Quality`, `Docs`, …).\n5. **`check` / preflight target** — validate required tools are installed.\n6. **Core targets** — install, test, lint, typecheck, clean, build, docs, etc.\n7. **Catch-all** (optional) — `%:` with a `@:` recipe when the Makefile accepts positional arguments.\n\n---\n\n## Emoji Conventions\n\nUse emoji as visual markers in `@echo` / `@printf` output to make progress scannable:\n\n| Emoji | Meaning |\n|-------|---------|\n| ✅ | Success / check passed |\n| ❌ | Failure / check failed |\n| 🧪 | Running tests |\n| 🧹 | Linting |\n| 🔍 | Type-checking |\n| 🧼 | Cleaning artifacts |\n| 📦 | Building / packaging / installing |\n| 🔄 | Reinstalling |\n| 🪝 | Pre-commit hooks |\n| 🔒 | Boundary / safety checks |\n| 👷🏻 | Building docs |\n| 🌐 | Serving / networking |\n\n---\n\n## ANSI Color Reference\n\n| Code | Color | Usage |\n|------|-------|-------|\n| `\\033[1m` | Bold | Help banner |\n| `\\033[0m` | Reset | End of styled text |\n| `\\033[1;38;5;208m` | Bold orange (256-color) | `##@` section headers |\n| `\\033[97m` | Bright white | Target names |\n| `\\033[32m` | Green | Success messages |\n| `\\033[31m` | Red | Error messages |\n\nOrange headers + white target names is the standard scheme — warm, high-contrast, and readable on\nboth light and dark backgrounds. The `38;5;208` 256-color code works in every modern terminal.\n\n---\n\n## Anti-Patterns\n\n- **No `##` comment on a user-facing target** — it won't appear in `make help`.\n- **Piping the help listing through `sort`** — breaks source order and `##@` grouping.\n- **`echo` for ANSI escapes** — behavior varies across shells; always use `printf`.\n- **Hardcoding tool paths** — use `?=` so users can override (`POETRY ?= poetry`).\n- **Spaces for recipe indentation** — Makefiles **require tabs**.\n---\napplyTo: \"**\"\ndescription: \"Repository-wide whitespace, EOF, and general file hygiene rules.\"\n---\n\n# General File Standards\n\nThese standards apply to **all file types** (Python, Markdown, YAML, TOML, JSON, Makefiles, etc.) in\nthis repository.\n\n---\n\n## Whitespace & Line Endings\n\n- **No trailing whitespace** on any line in any file type.\n- **Blank lines must contain no spaces or tabs.**\n- **Every file must end with exactly one newline.**\n\nThese three are enforced by the `trailing-whitespace` and `end-of-file-fixer` pre-commit hooks — run\n`make precommit` (or install the hook once with `make precommit-install`) to apply them automatically.\n\n---\n\n## Line Length\n\n- **120 characters maximum** for Python and Markdown. Reflow long prose to stay within the limit.\n- Other formats: follow the language/format convention (Makefiles use tabs for recipes; YAML/TOML as\n  the format dictates).\n\n---\n\n## When to Apply These Standards\n\n- **New files:** must comply with all standards from creation.\n- **Modified files:** only the modified sections need to comply — do not reformat unrelated regions\n  unless explicitly requested.\n---\napplyTo: \"**/*.md\"\ndescription: \"Markdown formatting rules (MyST-flavored, for the Sphinx docs site).\"\n---\n\n# Markdown Standards\n\nDocumentation is authored in **Markdown (MyST-Parser)** and built by **Sphinx**. Keep Markdown clean\nand consistently formatted.\n\n---\n\n## Line Length\n\n- **120 characters maximum** (see `general.instructions.md` for whitespace/EOF rules).\n- Reflow long lines at logical points (after sentences, before lists).\n\n---\n\n## Formatting Rules\n\n### Headings\n\n- **Surround headings with blank lines** (blank line before and after).\n\n### Lists\n\n- **Surround lists with blank lines** (blank line before the first item and after the last).\n\n### Consecutive bold / key-value lines\n\n- **Separate them with blank lines** if each should render on its own line. Adjacent lines with only a\n  single newline merge into one paragraph — the most common rendering bug.\n\n  ```markdown\n  <!-- Correct: each renders on its own line -->\n  **Transport:** BLE\n\n  **Codec:** length-prefixed frame\n\n  <!-- Incorrect: both merge into one paragraph -->\n  **Transport:** BLE\n  **Codec:** length-prefixed frame\n  ```\n\n### URLs\n\n- **Use `[text](url)` link syntax**, not bare URLs.\n\n### Code blocks\n\n- Surround fenced code blocks with blank lines; always specify a language for syntax highlighting.\n\n### Mermaid diagrams\n\n- Diagrams render via `sphinxcontrib-mermaid` — use a fenced ` ```mermaid ` block.\n- Mermaid label lines often exceed 120 characters; that is acceptable inside the fence. If a\n  line-length linter is later added, wrap the block in `<!-- markdownlint-disable MD013 -->` /\n  `<!-- markdownlint-enable MD013 -->` directives rather than globally relaxing the limit.\n\n---\n\n## MyST Notes\n\n- Cross-references, admonitions, and directives use MyST syntax (e.g. a fenced ` ```{note} ` block).\n  Prefer plain Markdown where possible; reach for MyST directives only when you need Sphinx features.\n- Build the docs to catch errors: `make build-docs` (or `make build-docs-strict` for `-W` /\n  warnings-as-errors).\n\n---\n\n## Quick Checklist\n\nBefore submitting Markdown:\n\n- [ ] Lines ≤ 120 characters\n- [ ] Headings surrounded by blank lines\n- [ ] Lists surrounded by blank lines\n- [ ] Fenced code blocks surrounded by blank lines, with a language tag\n- [ ] URLs use `[text](url)` syntax\n- [ ] `make build-docs-strict` passes for files under `docs/`\n# Kandra — Copilot Instructions\n\n> **Read [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md) first.** It is the agent-agnostic source of truth for this\n> repository's structure, tech stack, conventions, IP-isolation rule, and quality gate. This file only\n> notes how VS Code / Copilot picks up customizations.\n\n## Customization file layout\n\n| Form | Location | Loaded |\n|------|----------|--------|\n| Agent-agnostic instructions | `AGENTS.md` (repo root) | Always |\n| Copilot-specific notes | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` (this file) | Always |\n| File-scoped instructions | `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` | Auto-attached via `applyTo` glob |\n\nThe file-scoped instructions auto-attach by glob:\n\n- `general.instructions.md` (`**`) — whitespace, EOF, line length.\n- `python.instructions.md` (`**/*.py`) — ruff, mypy strict, typing, docstrings, async, testing.\n- `markdown.instructions.md` (`**/*.md`) — MyST / Sphinx Markdown formatting.\n- `makefile.instructions.md` (`**/Makefile,**/*.mk`) — self-documenting help, colors, standard targets.\n\n## Before generating code\n\n- Match the existing stack: **Poetry monorepo**, **ruff + ruff-format + mypy strict**,\n  **pytest + pytest-asyncio**, **Sphinx / MyST** docs, **pydantic v2**, async-first.\n- Run `make qa` before considering a change complete.\n- Keep the repo **IP-isolated**: no proprietary vendor names, device codenames, or copied third-party\n  code — example devices are fictional. See `AGENTS.md` → \"IP Isolation\".\n",

  }
}

Use the user's America/Los_Angeles date.\n- Record the game version and, when available, the source commit or build identifier.\n- Capture only the game window, avoiding unrelated desktop content. Use the approved computer-use screenshot tool.\n- Keep the storybook in the project, outside ignored build/scratch folders, and exclude it from Godot game imports.\n- If capture is blocked, record the gap honestly and preserve the build for later capture; do not fabricate screenshots.\n\n## Bestiary maintenance\n\n- Keep `bestiary/bestiary.html` current when adding or revising a monster, its artwork, or implementation status.\n- Give every creature a name, description, one gallery portrait, and links to game sprites and animation information.\n- Maintain separate pixel-art game sprites and hyperrealistic marketing portraits for each creature.\n- Store marketing portraits in `bestiary/<creature>/` with versioned filenames and preserve exact generation prompts.\n- Name creature folders after the monster using lowercase hyphenated names. Each contains `monster.json`.\n- Treat `monster.json` as the source for names, descriptions, and backstories; synchronize the gallery and catalog.\n- Keep stable creature IDs when renaming. Metadata asset paths are relative to the project root.\n- Leave backstory text empty with status `pending` until the storyboarding agent supplies it.\n- Preserve earlier artwork. Keep `assets/bestiary/catalog.json` aligned with the gallery and current asset paths.\n- Distinguish animation source artwork from validated runtime animations and playable enemies from planned creatures.\n- Keep marketing assets excluded from Godot imports with `bestiary/.gdignore`; record actual image dimensions.\n\n## Makefile conventions\n\nRead [.github/instructions/makefile.instructions.md](.github/instructions/makefile.instructions.md)\nbefore creating or editing Makefiles. Reuse established helpers and command entry points before adding tools.\n- Keep changes scoped to the requested behavior. {
  "type": "commandExecution",
  "id": "exec-ed968b70-c380-4315-b9f6-b9b7d1958450",

    "text": "[preset.0]\nname=\"macOS\"\nplatform=\"macOS\"\nrunnable=true\nexport_filter=\"all_resources\"\ninclude_filter=\"\"\nexclude_filter=\"tests/*,builds/*,README.md\"\nexport_path=\"builds/Global Plumbing Initiative.app\"\n\n[preset.0.options]\ncustom_template/debug=\"res://.tools/macos.zip\"\ncustom_template/release=\"res://.tools/macos.zip\"\napplication/bundle_identifier=\"com.sfoley.globalplumbinginitiative\"\napplication/short_version=\"0.12.1\"\napplication/version=\"0.12.1\"\ncodesign/codesign=1\nnotarization/notarization=0\n---\napplyTo: \"**/Makefile,**/*.mk\"\ndescription: \"Makefile conventions: self-documenting help system, standard targets, ANSI colors.\"\n---\n\n# Makefile Standards\n\n**When creating or modifying Makefiles**, follow these conventions for a consistent, user-friendly\nexperience. This repository's root `Makefile` is the reference implementation.\n\n---\n\n## Self-Documenting Help System\n\nEvery Makefile **must** include a `help` target that prints colorized usage. Typing `make` or\n`make help` should show a scannable list of available targets.\n\n### How it works\n\n1. Each user-facing target's help text is an **inline `## Description`** comment on the target line.\n2. The `help` target runs a single `awk` pass over `$(MAKEFILE_LIST)` and prints targets in **source order**.\n3. `help` is the **default target** (`.DEFAULT_GOAL := help`, listed first).\n4. `##@ Section Name` lines render as **bold-orange** headers above the targets that follow them.\n\n### Template\n\n```makefile\n.DEFAULT_GOAL := help\n\n.PHONY: help\nhelp:  ## Show this help message\n\t@printf \"\\n\\033[1mProject — available targets:\\033[0m\\n\"\n\t@awk 'BEGIN {FS = \":.*?## \"} \\\n\t\t/^##@ / { printf \"\\n\\033[1;38;5;208m%s\\033[0m\\n\", substr($$0, 5); next } \\\n\t\t/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+:.*?## / { printf \"  \\033[97m%-20s\\033[0m %s\\n\", $$1, $$2 }' \\\n\t\t$(MAKEFILE_LIST)\n\t@printf \"\\n\"\n\n##@ Quality\n\n.PHONY: lint\nlint:  ## Run the linter\n\t$(POETRY) run ruff check .\n\n.PHONY: test\ntest:  ## Run the test suite\n\t$(POETRY) run pytest -q\n```\n\n### Rules\n\n- **Every `.PHONY` target users should invoke** gets a `## Description` comment.\n- **Internal/helper targets** (catch-alls, argument shims) get **no** `##` comment — that keeps them\n  out of the help listing.\n- The awk script preserves source order, so **order targets the way you want them to appear**. Never\n  pipe the help listing through `sort` — it breaks source order and `##@` grouping.\n- Target names use **lowercase kebab-case**: `build-docs`, `check-boundary`, `serve-docs`.\n- Bump the `%-20s` column width if target names are longer.\n\n---\n\n## Standard Sections (in order)\n\n1. **Header banner** — a file-level `# ── … ──` comment describing the Makefile (not rendered by help).\n2. **Configuration variables** — `?=` for overridable tools (`POETRY ?= poetry`), `:=` for computed paths.\n3. **Help target** — always first; the default goal.\n4. **`##@` section headers** — group related targets (`Environment`, `Tests`, `Quality`, `Docs`, …).\n5. **`check` / preflight target** — validate required tools are installed.\n6. **Core targets** — install, test, lint, typecheck, clean, build, docs, etc.\n7. **Catch-all** (optional) — `%:` with a `@:` recipe when the Makefile accepts positional arguments.\n\n---\n\n## Emoji Conventions\n\nUse emoji as visual markers in `@echo` / `@printf` output to make progress scannable:\n\n| Emoji | Meaning |\n|-------|---------|\n| ✅ | Success / check passed |\n| ❌ | Failure / check failed |\n| 🧪 | Running tests |\n| 🧹 | Linting |\n| 🔍 | Type-checking |\n| 🧼 | Cleaning artifacts |\n| 📦 | Building / packaging / installing |\n| 🔄 | Reinstalling |\n| 🪝 | Pre-commit hooks |\n| 🔒 | Boundary / safety checks |\n| 👷🏻 | Building docs |\n| 🌐 | Serving / networking |\n\n---\n\n## ANSI Color Reference\n\n| Code | Color | Usage |\n|------|-------|-------|\n| `\\033[1m` | Bold | Help banner |\n| `\\033[0m` | Reset | End of styled text |\n| `\\033[1;38;5;208m` | Bold orange (256-color) | `##@` section headers |\n| `\\033[97m` | Bright white | Target names |\n| `\\033[32m` | Green | Success messages |\n| `\\033[31m` | Red | Error messages |\n\nOrange headers + white target names is the standard scheme — warm, high-contrast, and readable on\nboth light and dark backgrounds. The `38;5;208` 256-color code works in every modern terminal.\n\n---\n\n## Anti-Patterns\n\n- **No `##` comment on a user-facing target** — it won't appear in `make help`.\n- **Piping the help listing through `sort`** — breaks source order and `##@` grouping.\n- **`echo` for ANSI escapes** — behavior varies across shells; always use `printf`.\n- **Hardcoding tool paths** — use `?=` so users can override (`POETRY ?= poetry`).\n- **Spaces for recipe indentation** — Makefiles **require tabs**.\nextends RefCounted\n## Presentation only: atlas frames stay independent of the existing collision geometry.\n\nconst BACKGROUND = preload(\"res://assets/world/basement-v1.png\")\nconst SEAN = preload(\"res://assets/sprites/sean-v2.png\")\nconst TONY = preload(\"res://assets/sprites/tony-v1.png\")\nconst TOILET = preload(\"res://assets/sprites/toilet-v1.png\")\nconst SEAN_HEIGHT := 72.0\n# Generated poses cross uniform cell boundaries. Never\n  pipe the help listing through `sort` — it breaks source order and `##@` grouping.\n- Target names use **lowercase kebab-case**: `build-docs`, `check-boundary`, `serve-docs`.\n- Bump the `%-20s` column width if target names are longer.\n\n---\n\n## Standard Sections (in order)\n\n1. **Header banner** — a file-level `# ── … ──` comment describing the Makefile (not rendered by help).\n2. **Configuration variables** — `?=` for overridable tools (`POETRY ?= poetry`), `:=` for computed paths.\n3. **Help target** — always first; the default goal.\n4. **`##@` section headers** — group related targets (`Environment`, `Tests`, `Quality`, `Docs`, …).\n5. **`check` / preflight target** — validate required tools are installed.\n6. **Core targets** — install, test, lint, typecheck, clean, build, docs, etc.\n7. **Catch-all** (optional) — `%:` with a `@:` recipe when the Makefile accepts positional arguments.\n\n---\n\n## Emoji Conventions\n\nUse emoji as visual markers in `@echo` / `@printf` output to make progress scannable:\n\n| Emoji | Meaning |\n|-------|---------|\n| ✅ | Success / check passed |\n| ❌ | Failure / check failed |\n| 🧪 | Running tests |\n| 🧹 | Linting |\n| 🔍 | Type-checking |\n| 🧼 | Cleaning artifacts |\n| 📦 | Building / packaging / installing |\n| 🔄 | Reinstalling |\n| 🪝 | Pre-commit hooks |\n| 🔒 | Boundary / safety checks |\n| 👷🏻 | Building docs |\n| 🌐 | Serving / networking |\n\n---\n\n## ANSI Color Reference\n\n| Code | Color | Usage |\n|------|-------|-------|\n| `\\033[1m` | Bold | Help banner |\n| `\\033[0m` | Reset | End of styled text |\n| `\\033[1;38;5;208m` | Bold orange (256-color) | `##@` section headers |\n| `\\033[97m` | Bright white | Target names |\n| `\\033[32m` | ",

This repository's root `Makefile` is the reference implementation.\n\n---\n\n## Self-Documenting Help System\n\nEvery Makefile **must** include a `help` target that prints colorized usage. Typing `make` or\n`make help` should show a scannable list of available targets.\n\n### How it works\n\n1. Each user-facing target's help text is an **inline `## Description`** comment on the target line.\n2. The `help` target runs a single `awk` pass over `$(MAKEFILE_LIST)` and prints targets in **source order**.\n3. `help` is the **default target** (`.DEFAULT_GOAL := help`, listed first).\n4. `##@ Section Name` lines render as **bold-orange** headers above the targets that follow them.\n\n### Template\n\n```makefile\n.DEFAULT_GOAL := help\n\n.PHONY: help\nhelp:  ## Show this help message\n\t@printf \"\\n\\033[1mProject — available targets:\\033[0m\\n\"\n\t@awk 'BEGIN {FS = \":.*?## \"} \\\n\t\t/^##@ / { printf \"\\n\\033[1;38;5;208m%s\\033[0m\\n\", substr($$0, 5); next } \\\n\t\t/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+:.*?## / { printf \"  \\033[97m%-20s\\033[0m %s\\n\", $$1, $$2 }' \\\n\t\t$(MAKEFILE_LIST)\n\t@printf \"\\n\"\n\n##@ Quality\n\n.PHONY: lint\nlint:  ## Run the linter\n\t$(POETRY) run ruff check .\n\n.PHONY: test\ntest:  ## Run the test suite\n\t$(POETRY) run pytest -q\n```\n\n### Rules\n\n- **Every `.PHONY` target users should invoke** gets a `## Description` comment.\n- **Internal/helper targets** (catch-alls, argument shims) get **no** `##` comment — that keeps them\n  out of the help listing.\n- The awk script preserves source order, so **order targets the way you want them to appear**. Never\n  pipe the help listing through `sort` — it breaks source order and `##@` grouping.\n- Target names use **lowercase kebab-case**: `build-docs`, `check-boundary`, `serve-docs`.\n- Bump the `%-20s` column width if target names are longer.\n\n---\n\n## Standard Sections (in order)\n\n1. **Header banner** — a file-level `# ── … ──` comment describing the Makefile (not rendered by help).\n2. **Configuration variables** — `?=` for overridable tools (`POETRY ?= poetry`), `:=` for computed paths.\n3. **Help target** — always first; the default goal.\n4. **`##@` section headers** — group related targets (`Environment`, `Tests`, `Quality`, `Docs`, …).\n5. **`check` / preflight target** — validate required tools are installed.\n6. **Core targets** — install, test, lint, typecheck, clean, build, docs, etc.\n7. **Catch-all** (optional) — `%:` with a `@:` recipe when the Makefile accepts positional arguments.\n\n---\n\n## Emoji Conventions\n\nUse emoji as visual markers in `@echo` / `@printf` output to make progress scannable:\n\n| Emoji | Meaning |\n|-------|---------|\n| ✅ | Success / check passed |\n| ❌ | Failure / check failed |\n| 🧪 | Running tests |\n| 🧹 | Linting |\n| 🔍 | Type-checking |\n| 🧼 | Cleaning artifacts |\n| 📦 | Building / packaging / installing |\n| 🔄 | Reinstalling |\n| 🪝 | Pre-commit hooks |\n| 🔒 | Boundary / safety checks |\n| 👷🏻 | Building docs |\n| 🌐 | Serving / networking |\n\n---\n\n## ANSI Color Reference\n\n| Code | Color | Usage |\n|------|-------|-------|\n| `\\033[1m` | Bold | Help banner |\n| `\\033[0m` | Reset | End of styled text |\n| `\\033[1;38;5;208m` | Bold orange (256-color) | `##@` section headers |\n| `\\033[97m` | Bright white | Target names |\n| `\\033[32m` | Green | Success messages |\n| `\\033[31m` | Red | Error messages |\n\nOrange headers + white target names is the standard scheme — warm, high-contrast, and readable on\nboth light and dark backgrounds. The `38;5;208` 256-color code works in every modern terminal.\n\n---\n\n## Anti-Patterns\n\n- **No `##` comment on a user-facing target** — it won't appear in `make help`.\n- **Piping the help listing through `sort`** — breaks source order and `##@` grouping.\n- **`echo` for ANSI escapes** — behavior varies across shells; always use `printf`.\n- **Hardcoding tool paths** — use `?=` so users can override (`POETRY ?= poetry`).\n- **Spaces for recipe indentation** — Makefiles **require tabs**.\nconfig_version=5\n\n[application]\nconfig/name=\"Drain Damage\"\nrun/main_scene=\"res://main.tscn\"\nconfig/features=PackedStringArray(\"4.7\", \"GL Compatibility\")\nconfig/description=\"First Day on the Job — movement and shooting prototype\"\n\n[display]\nwindow/size/viewport_width=960\nwindow/size/viewport_height=540\nwindow/size/mode=2\nwindow/size/window_width_override=1600\nwindow/size/window_height_override=900\nwindow/stretch/mode=\"canvas_items\"\n\n[rendering]\nrenderer/rendering_method=\"gl_compatibility\"\ntextures/default_filters/use_nearest_mipmap_filter=false\ntextures/canvas_textures/default_texture_filter=0\n\ntextures/vram_compression/import_etc2_astc=true\n[preset.0]\nname=\"macOS\"\nplatform=\"macOS\"\nrunnable=true\nexport_filter=\"all_resources\"\ninclude_filter=\"data/*.json,assets/portraits/emotions-v1.json\"\nexclude_filter=\"tests/*,builds/*,tools/*,README.md\"\nexport_path=\"builds/Global Plumbing Initiative.app\"\n\n[preset.0.options]\ncustom_template/debug=\"res://.tools/macos.zip\"\ncustom_template/release=\"res://.tools/macos.zip\"\napplication/bundle_identifier=\"com.sfoley.globalplumbinginitiative\"\napplication/short_version=\"0.28.0\"\napplication/version=\"0.28.0\"\ncodesign/codesign=1\nnotarization/notarization=0\n",

The selected title song is “It Takes A Hero” by Zane Little Music.\n\n- Open employee selection: Enter, Space, controller A, or Menu.\n- Toggle music: M or controller Y (remembered for this session only).\n- Return to title from pause or the completed-job screen: Q or controller B.\n- Quit from title: Escape.\n\nTitle artwork and its exact generation prompt are preserved in `assets/title/`.\n\n## Choose your employee\n\nAfter Start, choose with A/D, arrows, left stick, D-pad, or a mouse click.\nConfirm with Enter/Space, controller A/Menu, or CLOCK IN. Prototype 23: Tony has 4 contact-hit health and speed 270; Sean has 5 and speed 235. Sprites, weapons, projectiles, and firing sounds differ. Agreed next mechanics direction (October 13): Tony is quicker with less health and rapid, low-damage attacks; Sean is stronger with more health and slow, heavy attacks. Proposed starting balance, not implemented: Tony 75 HP and 270 movement speed; Sean 100 HP and 235 movement speed. The requested reciprocal 25% health differences conflict mathematically: 75/100 makes Tony 25% lower and Sean 33⅓% higher; 80/100 makes Sean 25% higher and Tony 20% lower. Prototype 23 uses a provisional 4/5 contact-hit ratio; final balance remains open. Agreed weapon rule: each plumber has an exclusive arsenal; Tony cannot equip Sean’s weapons and Sean cannot equip Tony’s. Proposed assignments and balance (damage / seconds between attacks): Tony — pipe wrench (melee, 12 / 0.30), drain snake (melee, 8 / 0.25), pressure gun (ranged, 6 / 0.15); Sean — demolition hammer (melee, 60 / 1.50), heavy plunger launcher (ranged, 24 / 1.00; revised October 14), pipe-bomb launcher (ranged, 60 / 2.00). These replace the earlier shared-tool proposal. Canonical ownership checks now reject another employee’s weapons and unsupported mechanics explicitly. Melee, loadout selection, and pipe-bomb gameplay are not implemented. BJ (Billy-Joe) replaces S.U.M.P. as the robot company owner in current selection, dialogue, and victory text. Playtest weapon fairness and character selection; no companion AI or co-op in this iteration.</p></li><li><h3>Menus + settings</h3><p>Delivered: original illustrated title screen, animated pixel lettering, keyboard/controller Start, title-sound toggle, and return to title from pause. Prototype 10 adds Tony/Sean selection using keyboard, stick, D-pad, or mouse. Prototype 13 uses first names only (Tony and Sean) in selection and dialogue. Screenshots pending permission for visual capture. Prototype 12 simplifies the title to Start / Controls / Quit and adds original keyboard/gamepad diagrams. Button hints live in Controls, with the approved exception of a visible dialogue Skip hint. Tutorial code is removed. Prototype 19 adds only the approved skippable story introduction. Prototype 11 softens Tony’s selection line to “Fourth-generation plumber. Limitless experience.” Still planned: saved settings, audio levels, and input remapping.</p></li><li><h3>Accessibility + difficulty</h3><p>Readable text, reduced motion options, clear non-color cues, generous checkpoints, and adjustable challenge.</p></li><li><h3>Progress + stability</h3><p>Save settings and mission progress; test focus loss, controller reconnects, restart, and fullscreen transitions.</p></li><li><h3>Playtest the whole job</h3><p>Record confusing spots, input feel, boss fairness, crashes, and frame pacing. Add regression checks for real bugs.</p></li></ul><p class=\"gate\">Done means: a new player can launch, understand, finish, and return to the game without developer help.</p></section>\nroadmap.html:162:“the company” for the employer until its name is selected. Tool-specific guidance\napplies when that tool is used, not as a requirement to add it to every project.\n\n## General engineering and file hygiene\n\n- Read existing code and configuration first. Reuse established helpers and command entry points before adding tools.\n- Keep changes scoped to the requested behavior. Avoid speculative abstractions, unrelated cleanup, and comments or\n  annotations added to untouched code. Comment why a non-obvious decision exists rather than restating the code.\n- Keep utilities cohesive, generic, and dependency-light. Preserve established package/import boundaries. Add public\n  re-exports only intentionally; internal helpers need not become public APIs.\n- Use named constants or enums for meaningful identifiers, opcodes, and status values instead of unexplained literals.\n- Text files have no trailing whitespace, truly empty blank lines, and exactly one final newline. Preserve required\n  format semantics and existing encoding/line endings. New text defaults to UTF-8.\n- Default to a 120-character maximum for Python, Markdown, and shell, including comments and banners. Wrap logically,\n  without routinely wrapping at 80. Do not split a literal or machine-readable value in a way that changes its meaning.\n- Follow existing language/format settings for other files. Preserve user changes and keep temporary artifacts in an\n  ignored scratch location, preferably the project's existing one. Do not add scratch output to source trees or commits.\n- Read complete relevant tool output. Recover from errors or truncation with a focused read, structured output, or a\n  suitable retry before drawing conclusions. Report unresolved gaps; do not present partial results as complete.\n- Use fictional, neutral examples for reusable code and documentation. Keep proprietary implementations, private names,\n  internal URLs, credentials, and business-specific behavior out of cross-project material.\n\n## Python\n\n### Formatting, typing, and imports\n\n- Use four-space code indentation and a **120-character** limit. Keep formatter/linter widths consistent when setting up\n  a new project; use an existing project's declared settings when different.\n- Type function parameters, return values, methods, and class attributes. Aim for strict type-checking quality; avoid\n  bypassing checks with unexplained `Any`, ignores, or casts. Honor deliberate project exemptions such as test fixtures.\n- Prefer `list[str]`, `dict[str, int]`, and `X | None` when supported by the project's Python version. Use postponed\n  annotations when the existing code or version compatibility calls for them.\n- Group imports standard library, third-party, then local, with blank lines between groups. Use the configured\n  Ruff/isort rules rather than manually fighting the sorter.\n- Preserve the supported Python version and package layout. Use the existing environment and lockfile; when the project\n  uses Poetry, run tools through that environment. Ship typing metadata when maintaining a typed library that uses it.\n\n### Docstrings and command-line tools\n\n- Document public APIs and complex behavior. Match the package's established convention: Google-style sections where\n  configured, or reST/Sphinx fields such as `:param:` and `:return:` where established. Do not mix or convert styles\n  opportunistically. For a new Python project without a preference, use Google-style docstrings consistently.\n- Keep indentation inside docstrings in multiples of two spaces; prefer four-space list continuations over three-space\n  hanging alignment. Explain important exceptions, side effects, and constraints without duplicating obvious types.\n- Prefer Click for new CLIs when already available or an appropriate dependency choice. Preserve existing CLI frameworks\n  and avoid adding a dependency for a trivial script. With Click, use decorators, `click.echo()`, option `envvar`\n  support,\n  and `context_settings={\"max_content_width\": 120}`. Keep help informative and consistent with actual behavior.\n\n### Async, models, and generated artifacts\n\n- In an async codebase, keep I/O asynchronous and avoid blocking the event loop. Keep sync/async bridges at deliberate\n  boundaries; do not scatter `asyncio.run()` inside library code.\n- When Pydantic v2 is already the model layer, prefer immutable models and `extra=\"forbid\"` where those semantics fit.\n  Preserve the existing source of truth; regenerate and verify dependent schemas when models change.\n- Update generators/templates instead of hand-editing derived output. Preserve established dependency boundaries between\n  authoring tools, runtime libraries, and generated artifacts; verify output remains self-contained as required.\n\n### Linting and tests\n\n- Run the project's configured lint/format/type checks. Ruff, Ruff format, Flake8, Pylint, and mypy are conditional on\n  the\n  project; they are not a mandatory combined stack. Prefer strict mypy standards where appropriate/configured.\n- Run independent checks as separate commands so each result is visible; do not chain Ruff and mypy with `&&` in an\n  interactive tool call. Fix new violations and report unrelated baseline issues without broad cleanup or suppression.\n- In pytest projects, use focused `test_*.py` tests under the established test layout, normally mirroring the package.\n  Test meaningful behavior and regressions, isolating network, subprocess, and host-state dependencies when practical.\n- Use the configured pytest-asyncio mode for async tests. Keep hardware, container, or external-service integration\n  tests\n  separate from the default offline suite and run them only when the task and environment authorize them.\n- Run relevant tests after library changes and the repository's required completion gate. Distinguish passed checks,\n  existing failures, skipped tests, and unavailable environments. Do not claim checks ran when they did not.\n\n## Makefiles\n\n- For new project Makefiles, make `help` the first/default target with `.DEFAULT_GOAL := help`. Included `.mk` fragments\n  should cooperate with the owning Makefile rather than overriding its default goal.\n- Put an inline `## Description` on each user-facing target. Omit help comments for private helper targets. Use\n  lowercase\n  kebab-case names, `.PHONY` for non-file targets, and actual tabs for recipes.\n- Group visible targets with `##@ Section Name`. Even a short Makefile can use one `##@ Commands` group. Keep the list\n  in\n  source order with a single awk pass over `$(MAKEFILE_LIST)`; never sort the help output.\n- Use a bold banner, bold orange section headers (`\\033[1;38;5;208m`), bright white target names (`\\033[97m`), and reset\n  (`\\033[0m`). When adapting an existing Makefile, preserve target behavior and its\n  default build contract unless changing them is part of the request; a narrow edit is not a mandate for a full rewrite.\n- Arrange configuration, help, then grouped targets.
