````json
{
  "type": "commandExecution",
  "id": "exec-ea16c4b1-42ab-49f9-af2b-c587c6173583",
  "command": "/bin/zsh -lc \"cat > design/first-call-action/report.html <<'EOF'\n<\"'!doctype html>\n<html lang=\"en\"><head><meta charset=\"utf-8\"><meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width,initial-scale=1\">\n<title>Drain Damage — First Level Redesign Proposal</title>\n<style>\n:root{color-scheme:dark}body{margin:0;background:#101923;color:#e9eee9;font:17px/1.65 system-ui,sans-serif}main{max-width:1050px;margin:auto;padding:48px 24px}h1{font-size:clamp(32px,5vw,56px);line-height:1.1}h2{color:#9cedcd;margin-top:48px}a{color:#9cedcd}p{max-width:88ch}.tag{color:#ffd67d;font-weight:700}.panel,figure{background:#192a35;padding:24px;border:1px solid #3b5360;border-radius:12px;margin:24px 0}img{width:100%;height:auto}figcaption{font-size:14px;color:#bdcbd0}table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;margin:20px 0}th,td{text-align:left;padding:12px;border-bottom:1px solid #3b5360}th{color:#ffd67d}.scroll{overflow:auto}li{margin:10px 0}.small{font-size:14px;color:#bdcbd0}\n</style></head><body><main>\n<p class=\"tag\">ENGINEERING PROPOSAL · OCTOBER 16, 2026 · NOT IMPLEMENTED</p>\n<h1>A busier basement.<br>A proper boss at the end.</h1>\n<p>Recommendation: keep Tony and Sean’s unique weapons, make both responsive, replace repeated stop-and-clear waves with forward-moving encounters, and finish with a playable Clogfather. Prove the combat in a short opening section before rebuilding the whole level.</p>\n<p class=\"small\">Consolidated from Level Design, Game Mechanics, Art and Storyboarding. Prototype 43 / 0.43.0 remains the playable build. Counts, tuning, new species and dialogue below are proposals, not approved implementation.</p>\n<h2>1. Faster kills and a more responsive Sean</h2>\n<p>Your report of a long wait between useful Sean shots matches a real design problem. The configured cooldown is one second; missing once, needing a second hit and waiting for projectile travel can make the exchange feel much longer. Tony currently needs seven hits for a full-health toilet.</p>\n<div class=\"scroll\"><table><thead><tr><th>Starter</th><th>Current</th><th>Recommended trial</th><th>Effect</th></tr></thead><tbody>\n<tr><td>Tony’s pressure gun</td><td>6 damage / 0.15 seconds</td><td>12 damage / 0.16 seconds</td><td>Fast corrections and quick ordinary kills</td></tr>\n<tr><td>Sean’s heavy plunger</td><td>24 damage / 1.0 second</td><td>18 damage / 0.24 seconds</td><td>Heavier shots without a long penalty for missing</td></tr>\n</tbody></table></div>\n<p>Both trial starters deliver 75 theoretical damage per second while firing continuously. Keep current range, movement, health and lives for this comparison so we can judge the weapon change. This does not make the heroes equivalent: projectile speed, range, movement, durability and attack coverage still matter.</p>\n<table><thead><tr><th>Ordinary role</th><th>Trial HP</th><th>Tony hits</th><th>Sean hits</th></tr></thead><tbody>\n<tr><td>Light runner / swarm</td><td>12</td><td>1</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Flushfiend / standard runner</td><td>24</td><td>2</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Perched shooter / ambusher / ordinary flyer</td><td>36</td><td>3</td><td>2</td></tr></tbody></table>\n<p>At 240 pixels, a 24-HP enemy would take about 0.48 seconds for Tony or 0.70 seconds for Sean, including travel and assuming both hits land. Those are calculations, not playtest measurements. Bosses are explicit exceptions to the 1–3-hit rule. Avoid ordinary “elites” in the first comparison.</p>\n<p>Alternatives: give both starters identical 12-damage / 0.18-second cadence if you prefer identity entirely through weapon behavior; or use a stronger contrast of Tony 12 / 0.20 and Sean 21 / 0.35. The recommended middle option keeps the original flavor with much less waiting.</p>\n<h2>2. Continuous action with room to react</h2>\n<p>Replace six mandatory clear-all stops with continuous finite encounters, one deliberate machinery set piece and a boss lock. Missed enemies behind the camera must retire without being counted as kills or blocking completion. This requires changing progression logic, not merely adding enemies.</p>\n<div class=\"panel\"><strong>Opening trial: 12 enemies across 20 seconds</strong><p>Eight runners, one elevated shooter, one emerging threat and two flyers, plus a reachable airborne tool pickup. Start with forward arrivals, introduce a warned rear arrival, then layer an elevated attack and a marked grate entrance. The proposed 17-enemy opening is a later comparison, not the starting requirement.</p></div>\n<p>The 17-enemy plan needs roughly 39 Tony hits or 34 Sean hits with the proposed tuning. At 70% accuracy, that occupies about 8.9 or 11.7 seconds of trigger time, before movement and target switching. It is plausible on paper but leaves Sean less slack. Test it instead of assuming it is fair.</p>\n<ul><li>Initial screen budget: six visible threats, two shooters, six hostile projectiles. Count entry warnings and contact enemies, not individual decorative flies.</li><li>After validation: brief peaks of eight threats and ten hostile projectiles, no longer than five seconds. Keep two shooters and no more than three independent attack patterns.</li><li>Visible warning of roughly 0.6–0.9 seconds for new shooters/emergers; no offscreen aimed fire, no landing on the player, and a reachable escape lane.</li><li>Use action beats followed by short easing/traversal sections. Delay excess spawns; never release a backlog as a sudden burst.</li></ul>\n<p>Level Design’s full-route sketch contains 90 ordinary enemies across six spaces (17, 15, 14, 18, 16, 10). Treat 80–100 as an authoring budget, not a quota. Keep the 9,600-pixel route as a planning envelope and measure a 4–6-minute human clear; shorten empty stretches instead of padding enemy health.</p>\n<h2>3. Real structures, several fighting lanes</h2>\n<p>Use pipe bundles, pumps and supported catwalks to offer upper and lower routes. Required rises stay at or below 60 pixels, gaps at or below 80, and landing widths at least 120, then validate with both heroes. Their current jump reaches about 86 pixels.</p>\n<p>Catwalk tops need deliberate collision rules and clearance underneath. Background support columns can be decorative; clearly solid machinery blocks movement. Upper shooters must be reachable with the actual starter range and aiming angles.</p>\n<div id=\"mockups\"><p class=\"tag\">Art’s original concept mockups are being prepared. They will be inserted here before this report is delivered.</p></div>\n<h2>4. More behaviors without six new species</h2>\n<p>Keep Flushfiends as runners and the Septic Air Force as a non-hunting environmental hazard. Evaluate the existing Hallowed Widow art for an aggressive flyer, which still needs gameplay implementation.</p>\n<ul><li>New stationary shooter: floor mounts and elevated perches, with a clear windup.</li><li>New emerger: floor and ceiling variants sharing behavior.</li><li>New skirmisher: quick traversal with background or viewer-side entrance animations.</li><li>An optional fourth new species only if the Widow cannot fill the aggressive flying role.</li></ul>\n<p>Left/right arrivals, floor/ceiling emergence and depth entrances are presentation methods, not six species. A background or viewer-side monster stays harmless and untargetable until it reaches its marked gameplay position and settles. Only one depth entrance at a time; large foreground silhouettes must not hide the hero. Names and designs need Art/Storyboarding review.</p>\n<h2>5. Unique defaults plus exclusive pickups</h2>\n<p>Keep an unlimited default weapon and add one pickup slot. A flying tool crate supplies something usable by the selected hero, avoiding useless other-hero drops in solo play. Fire cadence belongs to each weapon, so Sean can eventually equip a rapid weapon.</p>\n<p>Initial concepts: Tony gets a pressure fan with three weaker bolts; Sean gets a short-range air ram with strong knockback. These are proposals, not approved weapons or available assets. Try a 20-second active-play duration, frozen during pause/dialogue/dispenser, with the default retained and the pickup lost on death. Duration versus ammunition, switching controls and replacement behavior remain decisions for the pickup trial.</p>\n<h2>6. The Clogfather is required</h2>\n<p>The redesigned level is not complete until both heroes can defeat a playable Clogfather. Toilet waves are no longer an acceptable final substitute. Use a low, reachable weak point, clear attacks, a broad fighting floor and a checkpoint immediately before the fight. Ordinary pursuit and lingering projectiles must not spill into the introduction.</p>\n<p>Start with a measured 45–60-second fight target, allowing longer imperfect attempts. Mechanics proposes 1,080 HP for the faster starters: 90 Tony hits or 60 Sean hits, roughly 14.4 seconds of sustained exposure. That is a tuning candidate, not a committed stat. Do not reach a duration target through long invulnerability or inflated HP; both defaults must work without pickups. Begin with one primary pattern, no more than six hostile projectiles and one summon.</p>\n<p>Completion must depend on confirmed boss defeat and stopped immediate hazards. Storyboarding’s proposed fact is “The Clogfather is down,” avoiding claims that all monsters are dead or plumbing is repaired. Draft endings have the other plumber on radio and BJ issuing another address. They remain unapproved dialogue; a usable exit and support character’s knowledge must be credible. No portal is assumed.</p>\n<h2>7. Build order and acceptance</h2>\n<ol><li><strong>Combat comparison:</strong> trial damage/cadence; measure input-to-shot delay, hit counts, missed-shot recovery and firing while moving/jumping.</li><li><strong>20-second playable opening:</strong> runner, shooter, emerger, one upper/lower structure and one pickup. Compare both heroes before increasing density.</li><li><strong>Full route:</strong> add flight/depth entrances, finite encounter scheduling, checkpoint-safe progress and approved art.</li><li><strong>Clogfather:</strong> attacks, art, phases, retry, defeat, appropriate ending and exactly-once mission completion.</li><li><strong>Playtest and polish:</strong> both heroes with defaults, controller readability, safe spawn lanes, performance/audio limits and a human full-route test. Build and capture actual screenshots with permission at each delivered iteration.</li></ol>\n<p>Engineering risks are manageable but substantive: current mission accounting assumes sequential clear-all encounters; current platform rectangles fill their whole footprint; enemy projectiles and pickup ownership need shared rules; the boss needs a real state machine. Automate those invariants, then use human playtests to judge pacing and fairness.</p>\n<div class=\"panel\"><strong>Recommended next decision</strong><p>Approve the direction and the short opening trial: faster distinct starters, 1–3-hit ordinary enemies, supported upper/lower paths, 12 opening enemies before testing 17, exclusive pickups, and a mandatory Clogfather finale. Treat the numerical values as trial settings rather than final balance.</p></div>\n<h2>Evidence and design records</h2>\n<p>Official Konami material describes weapon variety through spread, flame, homing, laser, bombs and alternate effects. Our inference is that attack pattern and pickups can distinguish heroes without forcing long firing delays. These sources do not supply our proposed HP, timing or density values: <a href=\"https://www.konami.com/games/contra/og/asia/en/\">Contra: Operation Galuga official overview</a> and <a href=\"https://www.konami.com/games/us/en/topics/2268/\">Konami’s announcement</a>. No Contra artwork, level layout or measured balance is being reproduced.</p>\n<p><a href=\"level-proposal.json\">Level Design proposal</a> · <a href=\"../../handoffs/first-level-run-and-gun-balance.json\">Mechanics tables, formulas and alternatives</a> · <a href=\"../../handoffs/level-one-redesign-engineering.json\">Engineering constraints and tests</a> · <a href=\"../../roadmap.html\">Roadmap</a></p>\n</main></body></html>\nEOF'",

Saved October 16, 2026.</p>\n<p class=\"note\">These are practical working definitions. Some are common industry terms; others, such as “emerger,”\nare useful shorthand for our project. They describe roles and behavior, not necessarily separate monster species\nor features already implemented.</p>\n<h2>Enemies and hazards</h2>\n<dl>\n<dt>Hunter</dt><dd>An enemy that actively seeks or pursues the player. Its movement responds to the player’s position.\nExample: a toilet monster that spots Sean and chases him.</dd>\n<dt>Emerger</dt><dd>An enemy that enters the action by coming out of something: a floor grate, ceiling vent,\nbackground hatch or even the space in front of the screen. This describes its entrance; it could become a hunter\nor shooter after arriving.</dd>\n<dt>Environmental hazard</dt><dd>A dangerous part of the space that the player must navigate around. It does not need\nto hunt the player. Examples: steam jets, electrified water or our wandering Septic Air Force swarm, which can harm\nboth plumbers and monsters. A hazard can be alive and destructible.</dd>\n<dt>Runner</dt><dd>A ground enemy that moves through a combat lane. It may follow a set route or pursue the player;\n“runner” alone does not specify which.</dd>\n<dt>Stationary shooter / perched shooter</dt><dd>An enemy that attacks from a fixed position. A perched shooter occupies\nan elevated position, encouraging the player to aim upward or take another route.</dd>\n<dt>Flyer</dt><dd>An airborne enemy. Its flight may follow a pattern, wander or track the player; the term describes\nhow it moves rather than how aggressive it is.</dd>\n<dt>Skirmisher</dt><dd>A mobile enemy that attacks briefly, then retreats or repositions. It pressures the player\nthrough movement rather than standing still and absorbing shots.</dd>\n<dt>Fodder</dt><dd>Relatively easy ordinary enemies that die quickly and keep action moving. They can still be dangerous\nin combination with other threats.</dd>\n<dt>Elite</dt><dd>An occasional, clearly distinguishable enemy with greater durability or more demanding attacks\nthan ordinary enemies. It should not be used as an excuse to make every monster slow to kill.</dd>\n<dt>Boss</dt><dd>A major encounter with distinctive attacks, usually marking a level’s climax. The Clogfather is the\nrequired boss for our proposed first-level redesign.</dd>\n</dl>\n<h2>Readable, fair action</h2>\n<dl>\n<dt>Telegraph</dt><dd>A warning before danger: a windup, flashing grate, shadow, sound or landing marker that gives\nthe player time to react.</dd>\n<dt>Windup / attack / recovery</dt><dd>The preparation, dangerous action and settling period of an attack.\nRecovery often gives the player an opportunity to retaliate or reposition.</dd>\n<dt>Attack pattern</dt><dd>A recognizable sequence or arrangement of attacks, such as a low projectile followed\nby a high one. Players learn patterns and find ways through them.</dd>\n<dt>Combat lane / escape lane</dt><dd>A route through the action. A combat lane carries movement or attacks;\nan escape lane leaves the player a reachable way to avoid danger.</dd>\n<dt>Play plane</dt><dd>The depth layer where normal gameplay collisions happen in our side-scroller.\nA monster can appear in the background before entering this layer and becoming dangerous.</dd>\n<dt>Hitbox / hurtbox</dt><dd>A hitbox defines where an attack can connect. A hurtbox defines where a character can\nreceive that hit. Neither has to match every visible pixel of the artwork.</dd>\n<dt>Invulnerability frames (“i-frames”)</dt><dd>A short period when a character cannot take damage, such as the\nprotection immediately after being hit.</dd>\n</dl>\n<h2>Level flow and balance</h2>\n<dl>\n<dt>Encounter</dt><dd>A designed stretch of action involving enemies, terrain and objectives.</dd>\n<dt>Wave</dt><dd>A group of enemies introduced together or in a scheduled sequence.</dd>\n<dt>Set piece</dt><dd>A specially arranged, memorable sequence, such as fighting through a pump failure while\nmachinery opens a route.</dd>\n<dt>Pacing / pressure and release</dt><dd>How intensity changes over time. Busy combat alternates with lighter\nmovement or recovery so the entire level does not feel equally exhausting.</dd>\n<dt>Threat budget</dt><dd>A limit on how much danger may be active at once: enemies, shooters, projectiles or\nindependent attack patterns. Many visible creatures need not all attack simultaneously.</dd>\n<dt>Encounter director</dt><dd>The game logic that schedules enemies and attacks while respecting progression,\nsafe entrances and threat limits.</dd>\n<dt>Fire cadence</dt><dd>The rhythm or interval between shots. A 0.25-second interval allows four shots per second\nwhile firing continuously.</dd>\n<dt>Time to kill (TTK)</dt><dd>How long it takes to defeat a target under stated conditions. Distance, misses,\narmor and aiming can make real encounters longer than a simple damage calculation.</dd>\n<dt>Damage per second (DPS)</dt><dd>A measure of sustained damage output. Equal DPS does not guarantee equal feel:\none weapon may fire frequent light shots while another fires fewer heavy shots.</dd>\n<dt>Pickup</dt><dd>An item collected during play, such as a temporary weapon, health or ammunition.\nAn exclusive pickup can be equipped only by its intended hero.</dd>\n<dt>Blockout / graybox</dt><dd>A rough playable layout made with simple shapes to test movement, routes and combat\nbefore investing in finished scenery.</dd>\n<dt>Vertical slice</dt><dd>A small representative section combining the main systems well enough to judge the intended\nexperience. “Vertical” refers to covering those systems, not to the level scrolling upward.</dd>\n</dl>\n<p><a href=\"../roadmap.html\">Roadmap</a> · <a href=\"first-call-action/report.html\">First-level redesign proposal</a></p>\n</main></body></html>\nEOF\npython3 - <<'\"'PY'\nfrom pathlib import Path\nfrom html.parser import HTMLParser\np=Path('roadmap.html');s=p.read_text();marker='<p class=\\\"intro\\\">';note='<p><a href=\\\"design/game-design-glossary.html\\\">Game design glossary</a> — our shared terms for enemy roles, fair combat, level flow and balance.</p>\\\\n'\nif 'design/game-design-glossary.html' not in s:s=s.replace(marker,note+marker,1)\np.write_text(s)\np=Path('design/game-design-glossary.html');s=p.read_text();HTMLParser().feed(s)\nassert s.endswith('\\\\n') and not s.endswith('\\\\n\\\\n')\nassert all(line == line.rstrip() for line in s.splitlines())\nprint('Glossary HTML and text hygiene checked; roadmap link added.')\nPY\"",

Sean approved the faster short-opening trial on October 16 and the sewer-system concept as the production visual direction. Shooter/emerger character art and validated flyer frames remain missing; Art has been asked to finish that work. Engineering can begin environment/runner integration, but the complete multi-role trial is not ready. Results will report actual issued enemies and safety deferrals; the test runway is not the final level length. The trial will be selected explicitly; the existing full-level balance stays unchanged. Only one Clogfather may appear at a time; omit the simultaneous background silhouette. Expand the route after the opening feels right. Recommended starter values are approved for the initial comparison, not final balance; new roster identities and pickup details remain provisional. Prototype 43 stays the current playable build.</p>\n<p><strong>Prototype 40 — larger fly swarms:</strong> Swarm artwork is twice as wide and tall (128×128 display canvas), including death animation; center registration and contact core stay unchanged. Optional health bars move above the enlarged art. Includes the approved BJ completion-line revision with neutral portrait. Export/signing and packaged swarm/completion checks pass; visual review and screenshots await permission.</p>\n<p><strong>Run-cycle revision:</strong> Both heroes have revised eight-frame run candidates, including a separately redrawn opposite stride. packaged lifecycle checks pass; listening pending\",\n  \"manifest\": \"audio/sources/sewer-fly-buzz-v1/manifest.json\",\n  \"runtime\": \"assets/audio/sfx/sewer-fly-buzz-v1/swarm-loop.wav\",\n  \"requirements\": [\n    \"Loop near living swarms only with distance attenuation and gentle entry/exit fades.\",\n    \"Cap simultaneous voices/total volume so swarms do not drown music or combat.\",\n    \"Stop on swarm death, restart and menu/level exit; pause with gameplay; honor SFX mute.\",\n    \"No trigger every frame; maintain one voice per audible swarm or one aggregate voice.\"\n  ],\n  \"menu_candidates\": \"audio/sources/menu-navigation-candidates-v1/manifest.json\",\n  \"menu_status\": \"Sean selected wrench clink October 16; ready for Engineering integration\",\n  \"menu_behavior\": \"Use selected cue on successful directional navigation in all pre-game screens; keyboard and controller share behavior. Avoid duplicate cues or uncontrolled held-key repetition.\",\n  \"menu_selected\": {\n    \"id\": \"wrench-clink\",\n    \"date\": \"2026-10-16\",\n    \"runtime\": \"assets/audio/sfx/menu-navigation-v1/wrench-clink.wav\",\n    \"sha256\": \"718bed01a9fa2d0d36541b313f39e6f3f5e757174328756a25918eb9bdbe2dde\",\n    \"integration_status\": \"ready_for_engineering\",\n    \"duration_seconds\": 0.24,\n    \"gain_db\": 0,\n    \"peak_dbfs\": -15,\n    \"loop\": false,\n    \"license\": \"CC0-1.0\",\n    \"author\": \"Kenney\",\n    \"source\": \"https://kenney.nl/assets/impact-sounds\"\n  }\n}\nwrench-clink.wav\n",

  }

Each user-facing target's help text is an **inline `## Description`** comment on the target line.\n2. The `help` target runs a single `awk` pass over `$(MAKEFILE_LIST)` and prints targets in **source order**.\n3. `help` is the **default target** (`.DEFAULT_GOAL := help`, listed first).\n4. `##@ Section Name` lines render as **bold-orange** headers above the targets that follow them.\n\n### Template\n\n```makefile\n.DEFAULT_GOAL := help\n\n.PHONY: help\nhelp:  ## Show this help message\n\t@printf \"\\n\\033[1mProject — available targets:\\033[0m\\n\"\n\t@awk 'BEGIN {FS = \":.*?## \"} \\\n\t\t/^##@ / { printf \"\\n\\033[1;38;5;208m%s\\033[0m\\n\", substr($$0, 5); next } \\\n\t\t/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+:.*?## / { printf \"  \\033[97m%-20s\\033[0m %s\\n\", $$1, $$2 }' \\\n\t\t$(MAKEFILE_LIST)\n\t@printf \"\\n\"\n\n##@ Quality\n\n.PHONY: lint\nlint:  ## Run the linter\n\t$(POETRY) run ruff check .\n\n.PHONY: test\ntest:  ## Run the test suite\n\t$(POETRY) run pytest -q\n```\n\n### Rules\n\n- **Every `.PHONY` target users should invoke** gets a `## Description` comment.\n- **Internal/helper targets** (catch-alls, argument shims) get **no** `##` comment — that keeps them\n  out of the help listing.\n- The awk script preserves source order, so **order targets the way you want them to appear**. Never\n  pipe the help listing through `sort` — it breaks source order and `##@` grouping.\n- Target names use **lowercase kebab-case**: `build-docs`, `check-boundary`, `serve-docs`.\n- Bump the `%-20s` column width if target names are longer.\n\n---\n\n## Standard Sections (in order)\n\n1. **Header banner** — a file-level `# ── … ──` comment describing the Makefile (not rendered by help).\n2. **Configuration variables** — `?=` for overridable tools (`POETRY ?= poetry`), `:=` for computed paths.\n3. **Help target** — always first; the default goal.\n4. **`##@` section headers** — group related targets (`E",

````text
# Project instructions

## Character names

- Use only Tony and Sean in all player-facing game text, including menus, dialogue, and credits.
- Do not add surnames to either character.

## Art collaboration

- Whenever new artwork is needed, ask the existing Bestiary / Art agent to help before creating it.
- This includes interface illustrations and props, portraits, environments, sprites, and replacement artwork.
- Engineering provides dimensions, layout constraints, and runtime requirements, then integrates the delivered art.
- Do not bypass Art by independently generating artwork or substituting code-drawn art without Sean's direction.

## Playtest window convention

- Before opening or foregrounding the game for Sean to playtest or inspect anything, ask permission and wait
  for an explicit yes. Explain what needs checking before asking. A general development request is not permission
  to interrupt him with a game window. An explicit request to launch or playtest counts as permission.
- After Sean approves, use a large, maximized window for his playtest.
- Keep agent-only checks headless or in the background when possible. If a visual test would steal focus,
  interrupt Sean, or require foregrounding the game, ask first; a small window is not an exception.
- When opening the game for agent-only testing or screenshots, use a small window; no user interaction is expected.
- Use a temporary launch override for agent testing so normal user launches remain large.
- Do not leave an agent test running in a large window unless explicitly handing it over for Sean's playtest.

## Build delivery and notifications

- After integrating game changes, including deliveries from other agents, build and run the relevant checks.
- Defer the build only when waiting for additional agent work that belongs in the same integration; tell Sean what
  is still pending rather than implying the new version is ready.
- Whenever a new build is ready, proactively tell Sean its version, what changed, and any remaining testing gaps.
- If a build fails, report the failure and do not describe it as ready to play.
- Building does not authorize opening or foregrounding the game; keep the playtest permission rules above.

## Roadmap maintenance

- Keep `roadmap.html` current whenever work is added, completed, changed, deferred, or reprioritized.
- Update affected descriptions, milestone order, statuses, remaining work, and current build/date as applicable.
- Make these updates in the same delivery as the work; do not wait for a separate user reminder.
- Distinguish partial progress from completed milestones and proposed ideas from agreed plans.
- Keep roadmap claims aligned with the running build and the development storybook.

## Development storybook

The user wants screenshots of every iteration to tell the story of the game's graphics and capabilities.

- For each delivered game iteration, capture actual screenshots of the running build before replacing it.
- Save original PNG or JPEG captures in `storybook/NNN-short-title/`, using the next three-digit iteration number.
- Keep earlier captures and entries intact; never overwrite an earlier iteration with newer artwork.
- Include a representative gameplay view and additional views when needed to show a new feature or milestone.
- Append a dated entry to `storybook/README.md` with embedded screenshots, a short narrative, new capabilities,
  and what is still placeholder or incomplete. Use the user's America/Los_Angeles date.
- Record the game version and, when available, the source commit or build identifier.
- Capture only the game window, avoiding unrelated desktop content. Use the approved computer-use screenshot tool.
- Keep the storybook in the project, outside ignored build/scratch folders, and exclude it from Godot game imports.
- If capture is blocked, record the gap honestly and preserve the build for later capture; do not fabricate screenshots.

### Making-of book curation

- Storyboarding owns ongoing editorial curation of the development storybook, coordinating with Engineering.
- Collect generous early, middle, and late development material for an eventual making-of book: milestone
  screenshots, before/after comparisons, character/menu/environment evolution, funny failures, and design pivots.
- Preserve earlier chapters and originals. Label concept art, rejected ideas, and actual gameplay captures distinctly.
- Engineering preserves builds and supplies actual screenshots under the existing permission rules. This standing
  collection request does not authorize opening or foregrounding the game without permission.
- Maintain a capture backlog for missing milestones so they can be photographed during an approved session.
- Timestamp every new storybook capture and making-of artifact with `YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS` in the filename and
  its entry/metadata, using `America/Los_Angeles` (for example, `20261016-233045-title-screen.png`).
- Record the timezone and UTC offset in metadata to disambiguate daylight-saving transitions. Distinguish actual
  capture/creation time from later archival/import time; add a suffix if filenames would collide within one second.
- Preserve historical originals. Backfill exact timestamps only from trustworthy capture records; retain known
  dates and mark exact times unknown when unavailable. File copy/modification time is not proof of capture time.

## Bestiary maintenance

- Keep `bestiary/bestiary.html` current when adding or revising a monster, its artwork, or implementation status.
- Give every creature a name, description, one gallery portrait, and links to game sprites and animation information.
- Maintain separate pixel-art game sprites and hyperrealistic marketing portraits for each creature.
- Store marketing portraits in `bestiary/<creature>/` with versioned filenames and preserve exact generation prompts.
- Name creature folders after the monster using lowercase hyphenated names. Each contains `monster.json`.
- Treat `monster.json` as the source for names, descriptions, and backstories; synchronize the gallery and catalog.
- Keep stable creature IDs when renaming. Metadata asset paths are relative to the project root.
- Leave backstory text empty with status `pending` until the storyboarding agent supplies it.
- Preserve earlier artwork. Keep `assets/bestiary/catalog.json` aligned with the gallery and current asset paths.
- Distinguish animation source artwork from validated runtime animations and playable enemies from planned creatures.
- Keep marketing assets excluded from Godot imports with `bestiary/.gdignore`; record actual image dimensions.

## Makefile conventions

Read [.github/instructions/makefile.instructions.md](.github/instructions/makefile.instructions.md)
before creating or editing Makefiles. These reusable conventions were brought over from Kandra:
self-documenting default help, source-order sections, orange headers, white target names, real tabs,
inline descriptions, and emoji progress. Preserve the Godot toolchain used by this game.

## Combat metadata maintenance

- Give every new monster a `health` object in its `monster.json`, including positive maximum and spawn HP,
  progression placement, health-bar visibility, balance rationale, and weapon hit-count comparisons.
- Follow `assets/bestiary/balance-policy.json`; compare both plumbers' available exclusive weapons.
- Mirror health summaries in `assets/bestiary/catalog.json` and the gallery. Keep design and runtime values distinct.
- Keep weapon mechanics in `weapons/<weapon-id>/weapon.json` and register each weapon in `weapons/catalog.json`.
- Bestiary owns each weapon's `game-art.json`; Marketing owns its `marketing-art.json`. Preserve versioned originals,
  exact generation prompts, dimensions, and implementation status. Store game art under `assets/weapons/`.

## Writing Style: Avoid Formulaic AI Copy

Avoid the repetitive use of paired sentence fragments,
especially in marketing copy, dialogue, descriptions,
headlines, and other creative writing.

Examples of constructions to avoid:

- "Two plumbers. One impossible job."
- "No tools. No backup. No problem."
- "One hero. A thousand enemies."
- "Teeth in the bathroom. Wings in the basement."
- "Small town. Big secrets."

These constructions rely on short, parallel fragments
placed next to each other for dramatic effect.

This style is overused in AI-generated writing and
quickly becomes repetitive and artificial.

Guidelines:

1. Prefer natural, varied sentence structures.
2. Use complete sentences where appropriate.
3. Vary sentence length and rhythm.
4. Avoid formulaic contrasts between two short phrases.
5. Do not default to movie-trailer or advertising-tagline
   language when writing promotional material.
6. Favor specific, original observations over generic
   dramatic constructions.
7. Paired fragments are not prohibited, but should be
   rare and used only when genuinely effective.
8. Before finalizing creative text, review it for
   repetitive rhetorical patterns and rewrite them.

The goal is natural, distinctive writing that does not
sound like generic AI-generated marketing copy.
````

SHA-256: `64639b8f5e6a8df6f8983277b79cf7a5a81c55ce1bf7eca2b3d389a8da672abc`

````text
---
applyTo: "**/Makefile,**/*.mk"
description: "Makefile conventions: self-documenting help system, standard targets, ANSI colors."
---

# Makefile Standards

**When creating or modifying Makefiles**, follow these conventions for a consistent, user-friendly
experience. This repository's root `Makefile` is the reference implementation.

---

## Self-Documenting Help System

Every Makefile **must** include a `help` target that prints colorized usage. Typing `make` or
`make help` should show a scannable list of available targets.

### How it works

1. Each user-facing target's help text is an **inline `## Description`** comment on the target line.
2. The `help` target runs a single `awk` pass over `$(MAKEFILE_LIST)` and prints targets in **source order**.
3. `help` is the **default target** (`.DEFAULT_GOAL := help`, listed first).
4. `##@ Section Name` lines render as **bold-orange** headers above the targets that follow them.

### Template

```makefile
.DEFAULT_GOAL := help

.PHONY: help
help:  ## Show this help message
	@printf "\n\033[1mProject — available targets:\033[0m\n"
	@awk 'BEGIN {FS = ":.*?## "} \
		/^##@ / { printf "\n\033[1;38;5;208m%s\033[0m\n", substr($$0, 5); next } \
		/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+:.*?## / { printf "  \033[97m%-20s\033[0m %s\n", $$1, $$2 }' \
		$(MAKEFILE_LIST)
	@printf "\n"

##@ Quality

.PHONY: lint
lint:  ## Run the linter
	$(POETRY) run ruff check .

.PHONY: test
test:  ## Run the test suite
	$(POETRY) run pytest -q
```

### Rules

- **Every `.PHONY` target users should invoke** gets a `## Description` comment.
- **Internal/helper targets** (catch-alls, argument shims) get **no** `##` comment — that keeps them
  out of the help listing.
- The awk script preserves source order, so **order targets the way you want them to appear**. Never
  pipe the help listing through `sort` — it breaks source order and `##@` grouping.
- Target names use **lowercase kebab-case**: `build-docs`, `check-boundary`, `serve-docs`.
- Bump the `%-20s` column width if target names are longer.

---

## Standard Sections (in order)

1. **Header banner** — a file-level `# ── … ──` comment describing the Makefile (not rendered by help).
2. **Configuration variables** — `?=` for overridable tools (`POETRY ?= poetry`), `:=` for computed paths.
3. **Help target** — always first; the default goal.
4. **`##@` section headers** — group related targets (`Environment`, `Tests`, `Quality`, `Docs`, …).
5. **`check` / preflight target** — validate required tools are installed.
6. **Core targets** — install, test, lint, typecheck, clean, build, docs, etc.
7. **Catch-all** (optional) — `%:` with a `@:` recipe when the Makefile accepts positional arguments.

---

## Emoji Conventions

Use emoji as visual markers in `@echo` / `@printf` output to make progress scannable:

| Emoji | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| ✅ | Success / check passed |
| ❌ | Failure / check failed |
| 🧪 | Running tests |
| 🧹 | Linting |
| 🔍 | Type-checking |
| 🧼 | Cleaning artifacts |
| 📦 | Building / packaging / installing |
| 🔄 | Reinstalling |
| 🪝 | Pre-commit hooks |
| 🔒 | Boundary / safety checks |
| 👷🏻 | Building docs |
| 🌐 | Serving / networking |

---

## ANSI Color Reference

| Code | Color | Usage |
|------|-------|-------|
| `\033[1m` | Bold | Help banner |
| `\033[0m` | Reset | End of styled text |
| `\033[1;38;5;208m` | Bold orange (256-color) | `##@` section headers |
| `\033[97m` | Bright white | Target names |
| `\033[32m` | Green | Success messages |
| `\033[31m` | Red | Error messages |

Orange headers + white target names is the standard scheme — warm, high-contrast, and readable on
both light and dark backgrounds. The `38;5;208` 256-color code works in every modern terminal.

---

## Anti-Patterns

- **No `##` comment on a user-facing target** — it won't appear in `make help`.
- **Piping the help listing through `sort`** — breaks source order and `##@` grouping.
- **`echo` for ANSI escapes** — behavior varies across shells; always use `printf`.
- **Hardcoding tool paths** — use `?=` so users can override (`POETRY ?= poetry`).
- **Spaces for recipe indentation** — Makefiles **require tabs**.
````

````text
# Drain Damage

A solo, forgiving 2D plumbing action prototype for macOS, built with Godot 4.7.2.
Bright retro visuals accompany adult dialogue. Choose Tony or Sean; BJ, the robot owner, supervises both.
Their employer’s working name is Mainframe Plumbing & Supply. The game title remains Drain Damage.

## Play

Open `builds/Drain Damage.app` in Finder. Godot is not required to play the exported app.
This local prototype is ad-hoc signed, not notarized for public distribution.

- Move: A/D or left/right arrows.
- Jump: Space (controller A). Release early for a shorter jump.
- Aim: WASD/arrows or controller left stick/D-pad; only straight-down aim requires being airborne.
- Fire: Hold Enter/Return (including keypad Enter). J and X also work.
- Pause/resume: Escape.

Prototype 45 starts the faster sewer opening directly from Start and continues through the 9,600-pixel first level.
There is no timed mode, twenty-second cutoff or results popup. The opening has supported one-way decks, clearer
foreground plinths, Flushfiend runners, a perched shooter, a warned floor emerger and flying spiders. Spatial triggers
and safety checks control arrivals; running past an unsafe entry does not create kill credit. Later rooms retain their
finite waves and checkpoints. Prototype 47 removes kill-count shutters: ordinary enemies never block advancement.
The finale remains toilet waves until the planned boss is implemented.

Tony has four contact-hit health and speed 270; Sean has five and speed 235. Both share jump physics.
One Spare Employee Dispenser near the midpoint saves progress and heals once. It holds one selected-hero clone.
Injured check-in plays a 5.5-second replacement gag; full-health check-in stamps in 0.4 seconds without using the clone.
The first replacement consumes its stock. Later respawns arrive beside the empty machine without another dispense.
Stock stays empty across deaths and revisits; only a new run refills it. The three-life system is unchanged.
Later injured sequences can use the existing dialogue-skip control. The gag costs no life. You begin with three total lives. After a death animation,
BJ presents one of twelve messages with a matching emotional portrait. Choose Continue to return to the latest
checkpoint with full health and three seconds of protection if lives remain. Held buttons cannot dismiss the popup.
Defeated enemies stay defeated. At zero lives, Game Over offers Retry or Return to Main Menu; Retry starts a fresh run.
Reach the exit; clearing ordinary enemy waves is optional. The approved introduction and route-specific completion dialogue remain skippable.
Prototype 35 animates body movement independently of aim, with six run frames and distinct jump, landing,
hurt and death poses. The HUD shows one selected-hero head for each remaining life.
Human pacing and visual review are pending. Automated tests verify continuous play beyond twenty seconds,
checkpoint recovery, encounter accounting, open traversal and completion conditions. They do not establish survival balance.
No game window is opened by headless tests.

## Opening screen

Prototype 12 opens with original illustrated plumbing chaos, a chunky pixel logo, subtle sparkles,
and Start / Controls / Quit. The Controls screen contains illustrated keyboard and gamepad references.
All in-game button instructions live there. The selected title song is “It Takes A Hero” by Zane Little Music.

- Open employee selection: Enter, Space, controller A, or Menu.
- Toggle music: M or controller Y (remembered for this session only).
- Return to title from pause or the completed-job screen: Q or controller B.
- Quit from title: Escape.

Title artwork and its exact generation prompt are preserved in `assets/title/`.

## Choose your employee

After Start, choose with A/D, arrows, left stick, D-pad, or a mouse click.
Confirm with Enter/Space, controller A/Menu, or CLOCK IN. Escape/controller B goes back.

| Employee | Weapon | Damage per hit | Time between shots | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tony: confident fourth-generation plumber | Pressure gun | 12 | 0.16 seconds | Fast recovery, lighter hits |
| Sean: idiot apprentice | Heavy plunger | 18 | 0.24 seconds | Heavier hits, slower recovery |

Tony is the default employee. The clipboard displays one profile at a time; the separate punch clock confirms it.
Restart and respawn preserve your choice. Return to title to switch employees. Balance is provisional.
The first-level profile supplies these faster values; canonical baseline records remain for comparison.
Tony’s pressure gun reaches 320 logical pixels; Sean’s plunger reaches 480.
BJ uses the approved server-rack portrait and semantic emotional expressions.

## Portrait dialogue

The tutorial and opening controls briefing were removed in Prototype 12. Character selection begins the approved story introduction, then the basement. Story conversations still freeze gameplay and support reveal, advance, and skip.
The expanded route is integrated. The Clogfather, acid hazards, and portal remain deferred.

The first world-art pass adds a layered pixel basement, animated Sean and toilet sprites, and detailed metal platforms.
Sean is completely bald with a chin-only beard and no moustache.
Idle, running, jumping, firing, and hurt poses are integrated; animation transitions still need polish.
Prototype 07 enlarges Sean to 72 logical pixels tall and fixes neighboring-pose bleed in the animation atlas.
The forgiving collision box stays unchanged; the projectile origin follows the enlarged launcher.
Portrait images were created with built-in image generation using the supplied likeness references.
The portrait prompts are preserved in `assets/portraits/prompts.json`.
World and sprite prompts are in `assets/art-prompts-v1.json` and `assets/sean-correction-v2.json`.

## Controller controls

- Move: Left stick or D-pad.
- Jump: A (hold for a higher jump).
- Fire: X or right trigger.
- Pause/resume: Menu/Start.

Bindings use Godot's standard gamepad mapping, with a stick deadzone to reduce drift.
Disconnecting a controller pauses play. Sean confirmed successful in-game testing with an Xbox Series X|S controller on
October 13, 2026.

## Develop

From Terminal, run `cd /Users/sfoley/repos/drain_damage`, then:

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `make` or `make help` | Show the colorized command list |
| `make check` | Check the Godot executable |
| `make build` | Build for the local OS; currently macOS only |
| `make build-macos` | Export, include license notices, ad-hoc sign, and verify the Mac app |
| `make build-all` | Build every supported export; currently only macOS |
| `make run` | Run current source in the normal large window |
| `make run-preview` | Run current source in a small agent-test window |
| `make editor` | Open Godot's editor |

Close the game before rebuilding. The Mac build replaces `builds/Drain Damage.app`.
`make run` uses the source directly, so it does not need a standalone export first.
Use `make run GODOT=/path/to/Godot` to override the executable. Paths may be shell-quoted if they contain spaces.
On macOS the default is the existing project-local Godot; other hosts look for `godot` on PATH.
Other-host execution is not yet verified. Windows will need a compatible shell and Make environment.

`make build-android`, `make build-ios`, and `make build-windows` are reserved commands that currently
fail with setup guidance. They do not claim to produce builds. SDKs, templates, signing where needed,
export presets, and real-device testing remain future work. Mac exports are not notarized for public distribution.

The project-local editor is in `.tools/Godot.app`. Import `project.godot` to edit the game.
The opening screen in `scripts/title_screen.gd` plays a repeating CC0 retro music cue.
Music provenance, adaptation details, and the Storyboarding brief are in `audio/title-music.json`.
The original recording and previous synthesized sting source are preserved under `audio/sources/`.
For small agent-only previews, launch with `-- --agent-test`; normal launches remain maximized.
Movement, combat, and synthesized sound are in `scripts/game.gd`.
Authored terrain and solid-body collision are in `scripts/first_call.gd`; finite encounter accounting is in
`scripts/mission_state.gd`. Art crops follow `assets/world/first-call/manifest.json`.
World rendering and sprite-atlas animation are in `scripts/world_art.gd`.

```sh
.tools/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot --path .
.tools/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot --headless --path . --script tests/smoke.gd
.tools/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot --headless --path . --export-release macOS
```

The official macOS template is installed in Godot's user export-template directory.
A local copy is also retained at `.tools/macos.zip`.
Downloaded tools, templates, build products, and Godot caches are ignored by version control.

## Git checkout and asset storage

Install Git LFS before cloning, then fetch the retained binary assets:

```sh
git lfs install
git clone https://github.com/jugglingbear/drain-damage.git
cd drain-damage
git lfs pull
```

Source, scenes, manifests, prompts, and documentation use ordinary Git. Retained images, audio, PDFs, and
source archives use Git LFS. Generated builds, downloaded tools, private likeness references, rejected artwork,
and obsolete magazine editions stay local and are excluded by `.gitignore`. The storybook preserves intentional
history. Some archived design records refer to excluded local drafts; those links are historical, not build inputs.

The initial commits organize the existing Prototype 52 snapshot by subsystem; they do not reconstruct its original
implementation chronology. The complete initial series is the buildable baseline.

For a fresh Mac checkout, install the Godot 4.7.2 editor and matching macOS export template. Place the editor at
`.tools/Godot.app` (or override `GODOT`) and the template at `.tools/macos.zip`, then run `make build`.
The tracked `licenses/GODOT_COPYRIGHT.txt` is copied into each exported app. Engine binaries and templates are
intentionally not downloaded by the build.

## Creative direction

- Solo play as Tony or Sean, with distinct weapons and a robot owner bossing both around.
- Cheerful SNES-inspired presentation, original characters and environments, adult language.
- Forgiving combat, quick retries, and readable attacks.
- Next milestone: playtest character selection and weapon balance, then develop the first mission and boss.

## Roadmap

Open the [development roadmap](roadmap.html) for milestones, priorities, and Android/iOS feasibility research.

## Development storybook

Follow the screenshots and milestones in the [making-of storybook](storybook/README.md).
Each delivered iteration adds a new chapter while preserving the earlier images.

## Credits and rights

Environment details and sound synthesis are authored in this project.
Background, character sprites, enemy sprites, and dialogue portraits use original AI-generated artwork.
No reference photos are bundled in the game.
The photographs serve as likeness references for character design. Confirm likeness and photo permissions before
release.

This game uses [Godot Engine](https://godotengine.org/), under the MIT license.
See [Godot's license and third-party notices](https://godotengine.org/license/).
Godot's bundled copyright notice is included alongside the exported app as `GODOT_COPYRIGHT.txt`.
Working names are provisional; no trademark or patent clearance has been performed.

## Combat metadata

Prototype 14 reads combat values from a generated, validated JSON bundle. Edit canonical specifications in
`weapons/<id>/weapon.json` and `bestiary/<slug>/monster.json`, then run `make combat-data`.
`make build`, `make run`, and `make run-preview` regenerate it automatically. `data/combat.json` is generated;
do not edit it. It is explicitly included in exports while the ignored marketing directories remain excluded.

The pressure gun and heavy plunger launcher use canonical damage, cadence, projectile speed, and maximum travel.
Flushfiends have 40 HP. Player health remains five points for both employees;
proposed player-stat changes are unresolved.
Ordinary enemy bars default off; toggle them on the Controls screen. The preference lasts for the session.
Damage rows use the approved exact boundaries, flash on every hit, and play death once, holding its final frame.

All six weapons validate, but melee, the pipe-bomb launcher, and loadout selection are not playable yet.
New weapon pixel sheets remain source artwork; current held weapons/projectiles retain their earlier visuals.
The Hallowed Widow has an animated damage preview and validated 80-HP data, not flight AI or playable encounters.
Its wing gutters and thorax alignment still need refinement. Runtime crop/anchor preparation is stored alongside
original damage specs; original images are preserved. Run the preview only when a visible window is appropriate:

```sh
.tools/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot --path . damage_preview.tscn -- --agent-test
```

Headless checks:

```sh
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_combat_metadata.py'
.tools/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot --headless --path . --script tests/combat_data.gd
```

The combat test deliberately logs rejected IDs, ownership violations, and unimplemented mechanics.

## Selected soundtrack

Prototype 16 uses “It Takes A Hero” for title/selection and “Hallow Quest” (16-bit) for the basement.
Both tracks are by Zane Little Music under CC0; source URLs, originals, licenses, and hashes are in
`audio/catalog.json` and each track's `audio/sources/<id>/track.json`. The earlier Face The Facts cue is preserved.

One music voice prevents overlap: fade out for 0.25 seconds, switch, then fade in for 0.25 seconds.
Title gain is -16 dB; level gain is -20 dB, with another 4 dB reduction during dialogue.
Hero repeats after its full ending rather than pretending to be seamless. Hallow loops its complete authored stream.
Music mute applies across screens; effects remain audible. Pause suspends music, restart continues it,
and returning to the title changes back to Hero. Headless tests pass; subjective listening remains pending.

## Dialogue emotions and current art

Prototype 18 integrates the Drain Damage title art and menu plates, Tony v3, Sean v4, and BJ v2 portraits.
Tony wears his navy work shirt in portraits; Sean has no glasses; BJ uses the beige server-rack design.
Title art and movement sprites retain their existing clothing. Marketing art is not substituted for game sprites.

Every conversation line has `who`, `emotion`, and `text`. Use semantic emotions from
`assets/portraits/emotions-v1.json`: neutral, happy, amused, sad, worried, afraid, surprised, angry,
skeptical, or embarrassed. Do not use numeric face indices. For example:

```gdscript
{"who": "TONY", "emotion": "skeptical", "text": "Four generations of plumbing. Still answering to a calculator."}
```

`scripts/portrait_library.gd` shares the 5×2 atlas selection between dialogue and character selection.
Rounded boundaries and clipped filtering prevent sampling neighboring cells. Headless tests validate all 30 cells
and both endings; final in-game portrait framing remains pending a permitted visual session.
Storyboarding's future spider conversation remains deferred until a spider encounter exists.

## Opening story

Prototype 19 plays the approved seven-line introduction after character selection, once per fresh new game.
The shared script in `scripts/story_dialogue.gd` uses canonical speaker IDs and named emotional tones.
Both characters participate regardless of the selected hero. Death, checkpoint respawn, and retry do not replay it;
returning to the title and starting a new game does. The ending dialogue is unchanged.

The dialogue overlay shows the current Skip binding (Tab or controller B). This is an approved exception to keeping
button hints on Controls. Typewriter reveal and advance remain; world simulation freezes during conversations.
Dismissal waits for held dialogue/shoot/jump buttons to release before action can resume.
Future between-level scenes will use the same conversation system; no future scenes or tutorial have been added.

## Controls field guide

Prototype 20 separates primary gameplay actions from job, menu, and conversation references. The keyboard and
rounded, unbranded gamepad use original grimy hardware illustrations; live text describes the actual bindings.
Music and enemy-bar toggles have separate clickable footer buttons. Keyboard/controller shortcuts are unchanged.
Artwork, exact generation prompts, dimensions, and reference-manual links are in `assets/controls/art-v1.json`.
Source illustrations use the built-in image-generation tool; source web artwork was not copied.

Two optional sewer-fly swarms drift through the first level without chasing. Each has 12 HP; contact can hurt
plumbers and ordinary monsters. They are not required for doors to open, and stay defeated across checkpoint recovery.
Their initial movement and contact balance still need visual playtesting.

## Version and release handoff

`application/config/version` in `project.godot` is the canonical `X.Y.Z` version. The main title and gameplay show
it as a small white-on-dark badge at the lower right, inside a 16-pixel inset. Controls and employee selection omit
it; dialogue, death, pause, and dispenser overlays can cover it. The current layout targets the 960×540 logical
canvas. Device-specific mobile safe areas remain untested.

`make build` synchronizes both macOS export version fields before exporting. After changing the project version,
run `python3 tools/sync_project_version.py`; use `--check` to reject drift. Direct editor exports must follow that
step too. Packaged validation compares the displayed project version with the app bundle metadata.

For a future explicit release request, the release-coordination chat collects readiness from Marketing (current
lore magazine), Bestiary / Art, Game Mechanics, Audio (level music, weapons, intended dialogue sound), and
Storyboarding (plot implementation, names, and backgrounds). Engineering integrates approved deliveries, records
remaining gaps, builds the supported targets, and verifies the packages. A normal prototype build is not a release
request and does not authorize a full platform release or release-binary upload.

### Platform readiness

- **macOS:** matching Godot export template, Apple Silicon support, codesign, and ZIP or DMG packaging.
  Local exports and headless checks pass. Ad-hoc signing only; fresh-machine installation and Gatekeeper review
  remain. Public distribution needs a signing/notarization decision.
- **Windows:** matching export template, x86_64 preset, EXE/PCK ZIP, and optional signing. No preset or Windows
  runtime test yet. Verify controls, audio, installation, and antivirus behavior on Windows.
- **Linux:** matching template, chosen x86_64/ARM64 preset, executable permissions, and archive. No preset or Linux
  runtime test yet. Validate the target distribution, graphics, input, and audio.
- **Android:** Android template, SDK/JDK, ARM64 preset, private signing key, and APK. No mobile build yet.
  APK sideload instructions and actual Android device testing are required.
- **iOS:** iOS template, macOS/Xcode, ARM64 export, Apple team/provisioning/signing. No mobile build yet.
  Choose Xcode development install, Ad Hoc, or TestFlight; device registration and account limits apply.

For mobile readiness, assess touch controls, alternative screen layouts, aspect ratios, cutouts/safe areas,
orientation, suspend/resume, audio interruptions, controller reconnects, performance, memory, and battery use.
Successful export is not evidence that a platform has been played or tested.

### Release packages and Git LFS

Continue using ignored `builds/Prototype-NN/` and `builds/history/` for everyday local builds. For an explicitly
requested release, prepare `dist/vX.Y.Z/<platform>-<architecture>/` with packaged binaries, installation notes,
checksums, source commit, tool/template versions, signing status, and actual test evidence. Keep the source folder
and uncompressed app bundles out of `dist`; package the Mac app as ZIP or DMG to preserve its metadata.

Release binaries must be tracked through Git LFS and pushed to the public repository when Sean requests a release.
GitHub Release downloads may supplement that storage, not replace it. Verify `git check-attr filter` for every
package, run `git lfs fsck`, and verify remote download hashes after pushing. Never include signing keys, credentials,
provisioning profiles, or private references. Existing ignore rules still exclude tools, local builds, and secrets.

Git LFS is installed and asset uploads to origin succeeded on October 16, 2026. Account quota remaining has not
been verified. Before releasing, check the owner's billing usage and budget: GitHub Free/Pro currently include
10 GiB each of LFS storage and download bandwidth; their per-file cap is 2 GB. Every changed binary version consumes
its full size, and downloads consume bandwidth. Do not enable paid overages without authorization. See
[GitHub LFS billing](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/git-lfs) and
[LFS file limits](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-large-files/about-git-large-file-storage).

### Source: Makefile

SHA-256: `6cec25ab32186efe42e4906165838a6690cafc4c844cb34c52be692c294480d4`

````text
# ── Drain Damage — local development and platform exports ──
SHELL := /bin/sh
.DEFAULT_GOAL := help
HOST_OS := $(shell uname -s)
ifeq ($(HOST_OS),Darwin)
GODOT ?= .tools/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot
else
GODOT ?= godot
endif
MAC_APP := builds/Drain Damage.app

.PHONY: help check build build-all build-macos build-android build-ios build-windows run run-preview editor combat-data

help: ## Show available commands
	@printf '\n\033[1mDrain Damage — available commands:\033[0m\n'
	@awk 'BEGIN { FS = ":.*## " } \
		/^##@ / { printf "\n\033[1;38;5;208m%s\033[0m\n", substr($$0, 5); next } \
		/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+:.*## / { printf "  \033[97m%-22s\033[0m %s\n", $$1, $$2 }' \
		$(MAKEFILE_LIST)
	@printf '\n'

##@ Commands
check: ## Check that Godot is available
	@command -v "$(GODOT)" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { \
		printf '❌ Godot not found. Set GODOT=/path/to/Godot (one executable, no arguments).\n' >&2; exit 1; }
	@"$(GODOT)" --version

build: ## Build for this computer’s OS (macOS currently supported)
ifeq ($(HOST_OS),Darwin)
	@$(MAKE) build-macos
else
	@printf '❌ No native export configured for %s yet. See make help.\n' "$(HOST_OS)" >&2
	@exit 1
endif

build-all: build-macos ## Build all currently supported exports (macOS only)

build-macos: check combat-data ## Export and ad-hoc sign the standalone Mac app
	@test "$(HOST_OS)" = Darwin || { printf '❌ Mac packaging requires macOS.\n' >&2; exit 1; }
	@test -f .tools/macos.zip || { printf '❌ Missing Godot export template: .tools/macos.zip\n' >&2; exit 1; }
	@command -v codesign >/dev/null 2>&1 || { printf '❌ codesign is required.\n' >&2; exit 1; }
	@python3 tools/sync_project_version.py
	@printf '📦 Importing assets and exporting macOS…\n'
	@mkdir -p builds
	@"$(GODOT)" --headless --path . --editor --import
	@"$(GODOT)" --headless --path . --export-release macOS "$(MAC_APP)"
	@cp licenses/GODOT_COPYRIGHT.txt "$(MAC_APP)/Contents/Resources/GODOT_COPYRIGHT.txt"
	@codesign --force --deep --sign - "$(MAC_APP)"
	@codesign --verify --deep --strict "$(MAC_APP)"
	@printf '✅ Built %s\n' "$(MAC_APP)"

build-android: ## Planned: Android APK (not configured yet)
	@printf '❌ Android pending: add SDK/JDK, export template, signing and Android preset first.\n' >&2
	@exit 1

build-ios: ## Planned: iOS Xcode project (not configured yet)
	@printf '❌ iOS pending: add Xcode, export template, signing and iOS preset first.\n' >&2
	@exit 1

build-windows: ## Planned: Windows executable (not configured yet)
	@printf '❌ Windows pending: add export template and Windows preset, then test on Windows.\n' >&2
	@exit 1

run: check combat-data ## Run current source on the local OS (normal large window)
	@printf '🎮 Running current source with the local Godot engine…\n'
	@"$(GODOT)" --path .

run-preview: check combat-data ## Run current source in a small agent-test window
	@printf '🎮 Opening small preview…\n'
	@"$(GODOT)" --path . -- --agent-test

editor: check ## Open this project in the Godot editor
	@printf '🛠️ Opening Godot editor…\n'
	@"$(GODOT)" --editor --path .

combat-data: ## Validate canonical combat JSON and generate exportable data
	@python3 tools/build_combat_data.py
````

# Global Plumbing Initiative: the making-of storybook

From the first plunger to whatever happens next. Each chapter preserves a playable iteration's real screenshots,
what it could do, and the rough edges that made it a work in progress.

## 001 — First day on the job

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 01 / 0.1.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app with Apple Silicon support

Sean's plumbing career begins as a handful of colored rectangles in a basement. Three toilets have developed
an attitude, Tony is supervising through commentary, and the company motto is already on the wall:
“No job too shitty.”

![Sean and three hopping toilets in the first basement room](001-first-day/01-service-bay.jpg)

### What came to life

- Running and variable-height jumping, with two platforms to try.
- A plunger launcher and three hopping toilets that take three hits each.
- Five health points, temporary damage protection, and unlimited retries.
- Synthesized sound effects, Tony's commentary, pause, restart, and a victory screen.
- A standalone Mac app that was tested through the victory condition.

### Still wonderfully rough

The characters are tiny procedural placeholder shapes. This is one fixed room, with no scrolling mission or boss yet.
Tony appears through text; his character artwork and story appearances are still ahead.

### Screenshot notes

Captured from the running exported Mac app after the first prototype was completed. This is an unedited game-window
capture, including the macOS window title bar. Earlier development steps were not archived as separate images.

## 002 — A little more reach, a better grip

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 02 / 0.2.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app

The first playtest found that the ledges asked too much of an otherwise satisfying jump, and firing with J or X
cramped Sean's operator. The jump physics stay the same; the platforms now sit lower and closer together.
Enter/Return takes over as the main keyboard fire key.

![Iteration 02: reachable ledges and revised keyboard and controller hints](002-better-controls/01-room.jpg)

### New capabilities

- More forgiving platform placement, verified by complete simulated jumps onto both ledges.
- Enter/Return and keypad Enter fire plungers; J and X remain available.
- Xbox-style controller mappings: left stick/D-pad to move, A to jump, X/right trigger to fire.
- Menu/Start pauses, Y restarts, and disconnecting a controller pauses the game.
- Stick and trigger deadzones reject small accidental inputs.

![Victory reached using Enter to fire in the exported Mac app](002-better-controls/02-enter-victory.jpg)

### Validation and remaining work

Enter firing was also verified through victory in the exported app.
Automated checks cover ledge reachability, keyboard firing, controller button/axis mappings, deadzones,
and disconnect handling. These are simulated input checks; a real Xbox controller still needs a hands-on playtest.
The artwork remains the original placeholder style, with no scrolling level or boss yet.

## 003 — The crew gets a face

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 03 / 0.3.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app

The visual pass starts early. Tony and Sean now have illustrated dialogue portraits, original work outfits,
and four expressions each. Tony ranges from professional confidence to exasperation and shouting;
Sean ranges from eager optimism to bewilderment, full panic, and sheepish relief.

![Tony explains the rules of the trade](003-portraits/01-tony.jpg)

![Sean confidently misunderstands the assignment](003-portraits/02-sean.jpg)

![Sean discovers that the toilet has ambitions](003-portraits/03-panic.jpg)

### New capabilities

- Large illustrated portraits over a dimmed game world, with speaker names and character-specific accent colors.
- Six-line opening conversation and a two-line victory exchange.
- Text reveal, advance, skip, and replay using keyboard or controller bindings.
- Frozen gameplay during dialogue, with a short input guard before returning control.

### Art direction and validation

Generated with built-in imagegen from the supplied likeness references. Source atlases and exact prompts are preserved
in `assets/portraits/`. The dialogue layout takes inspiration from the supplied example without copying its artwork.
Automated gameplay and dialogue checks pass; keyboard advancement and skipping were visually checked in the exported
app.
New dialogue controls still need a physical controller playtest. The world and player sprites remain placeholders;
more detailed pixel sprites and environment art are the next visual work alongside the scrolling level.

## 004 — Tony runs apprentice induction

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 04 / 0.4.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app

The basement becomes a tutorial. Tony introduces one action at a time through portrait dialogue, then disappears
while Sean tries it. Lessons complete through actions, not timers. The controls strip and floating jump labels are gone.

![Tony introduces movement and the yellow marker](004-guided-basement/01-movement-lesson.jpg)

![Tony introduces the plunger launcher](004-guided-basement/02-shooting-lesson.jpg)

![The camera follows Sean into the practice area](004-guided-basement/03-scrolling-practice.jpg)

![Tony explains the activated checkpoint](004-guided-basement/05-checkpoint-instructions.jpg)

![Sean reaches the end of training](004-guided-basement/06-training-finished.jpg)

### New capabilities

- A scrolling basement with movement, platform landing, firing, combined practice, checkpoint, and exit stages.
- Portrait instructions adapt to keyboard or controller input, with optional current-lesson reminders.
- Visible shutters separate lesson areas; each completed action opens the next section.
- Maintenance cabinet restores health and becomes the return point after defeat for the current run.
- Full tutorial skip opens the route while keeping combat, checkpoint, and exit functional.
- Health stays visible; no permanent controls banner interrupts the game world.

### Validation and remaining work

Gameplay, dialogue, and tutorial checks pass, including checkpoint recovery and skip behavior.
The exported Mac app was played through from movement instruction to the exit conversation using the keyboard.
Physical-controller playtesting of this new lesson flow remains for Sean. World and sprite artwork remain placeholders;
there is no boss or progress saved across app launches yet.

## 005 — Less talk, more toilets

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 05 / 0.5.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app

Sean's feedback reshapes induction: Tony gives one short controls briefing and lets the apprentice get on with it.
The game launches maximized. The toilets now roam farther, hop faster, and chase nearby apprentices.

![Tony gives a brief controller introduction](005-less-talk-more-toilets/01-short-briefing.jpg)

![Keyboard controls in the same short briefing](005-less-talk-more-toilets/02-keyboard-briefing.jpg)

![A roaming toilet closes in on Sean](005-less-talk-more-toilets/04-gameplay.jpg)

### New capabilities

- Immediately visible opening briefing, with keyboard or controller instructions.
- Free exploration without walking, jumping, shooting, or checkpoint dialogue interruptions.
- Wider toilet patrols and faster movement, with local pursuit when Sean approaches.
- Large launch window while preserving the game's aspect ratio.
- Five health points, damage protection, and automatic checkpoint recovery retain forgiving play.

### Validation and remaining work

Gameplay, dialogue, and tutorial regression checks pass, including patrol bounds and pursuit.
The exported Mac app was visually checked for window size, briefing layout, movement, and enemy contact damage.
The physical controller remains available for Sean's playtest of the updated pacing.
World and player artwork remain placeholders, with no boss or saved progress across launches yet.
Markdown lint tooling was unavailable locally; document whitespace and line widths were checked directly.

## 006 — The basement gets its first pixel-art pass

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 06 / 0.6.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app

The art milestone moves ahead of the first boss mission. Flat wall blocks become a detailed boiler basement with
brickwork, copper pipes, gauges, warm lamps, and layers that scroll at different speeds.
Sean gets an animated pixel sprite, and the toilets become angry porcelain creatures with little pipe feet.
The first Sean sheet incorrectly added side hair and a moustache. Sean caught it, and the integrated revision has a
completely bald head and a chin-only beard. The rejected sheet is not bundled in the game.

![The first pixel-art basement with Sean and a toilet enemy](006-first-pixel-art/01-basement.jpg)

![Sean after clearing the first encounter](006-first-pixel-art/02-combat.jpg)

![The maintenance area with its own sign and first-aid cabinet](006-first-pixel-art/03-maintenance.jpg)

### New capabilities

- Original generated background and transparent sprite atlases, integrated into the actual running game.
- Sean idle, four running poses, jump, fire, and hurt poses; mirrored correctly when facing left.
- Toilet walking, hopping, and hit poses, plus grounded shadows and updated plunger projectiles.
- Layered scrolling, decorative water drips, detailed platform edges, and distinct area signs.
- The company slogan appears only at the entrance.
- Art rendering is separated from movement and combat, preserving the existing collision geometry and controls.

### Validation and remaining work

Movement/combat, dialogue, and tutorial regression checks pass. The exported Mac app was checked for sprite scale,
left/right facing, combat, scrolling, and checkpoint-area readability. Its local code signature verifies.
Original screenshots above were captured from the game window. Earlier chapters are preserved.
This is the first art pass: animation transitions, foreground props, effects, and visual consistency
need further polish.
Tony's in-world sprite, defeat animation, boss mission, music, and saved progress remain future work.

Art was generated with the built-in image tool. Sources are in `assets/world/` and `assets/sprites/`;
exact prompts are in `assets/art-prompts-v1.json` and `assets/sean-correction-v2.json`.
Markdown lint tooling remains unavailable locally; whitespace and line widths were checked directly.

## 007 — A larger, steadier Sean

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 07 / 0.7.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app

Sean was too small, and an animation crop caused a visible vertical offset. The generated sheet was not a perfectly
uniform grid: the jump crop included a neighboring pose's boot. Explicit pose boundaries now isolate each character.
Sean is 72 logical pixels tall instead of 50, a 44% increase, while retaining his bald head and chin-only beard.

![Larger Sean at the entrance](007-larger-steady-sean/01-larger-sean.jpg)

![Sean standing on the first platform after jumping](007-larger-steady-sean/02-jump.jpg)

### Changes and validation

- Corrected jump and firing crops; running poses stay within two logical pixels of the standing height.
- Kept the forgiving collision size and movement physics; moved the shot origin to match the enlarged launcher.
- Sprite-alignment regression checks and existing gameplay, dialogue, and tutorial checks pass.
- Exported app checked for character size and platform landing; local code signature verifies.

The animation is still an initial small pose set, so smoother transitions and additional frames remain future polish.
Markdown lint tooling remains unavailable locally; document whitespace and line widths were checked directly.

## 008 — Stop the apprentice leaking

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 08 / 0.8.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app

Sean proposes a more appropriate healthcare plan: plumber's tape. The first-aid cabinet becomes a large tape roll
with a loose white tail and an amber rim that turns green when activated. The label changes to LEAK SEALED.
Tony explains the logic in the existing short briefing, without adding another interruption.

![Tony explains apprentice leak prevention](008-stop-the-leaks/01-briefing.jpg)

![The tape checkpoint is activated](008-stop-the-leaks/02-tape-checkpoint.jpg)

### Changes and validation

- Plumber's tape replaces the first-aid cabinet artwork and wording.
- Existing full-health restoration and checkpoint respawn remain intact.
- Checkpoint and tutorial regression checks pass; exported briefing and activated tape were visually checked.
- The local app signature verifies. Roadmap and player documentation reflect the change.

The tape is currently a stationary checkpoint, not a carryable consumable or wrapping animation.
Markdown lint tooling remains unavailable locally; document whitespace and line widths were checked directly.

## 009 — Press Start, call a plumber

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 09 / 0.9.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app

The opening screen moves ahead of the boss mission. Tony poses like an action hero, Sean panics with his plunger
launcher, and a giant toilet looms over both. Chunky pixel lettering, drifting sparkles, rotating silly slogans,
and an original synthesized chiptune sting give the game a nostalgic introduction.

![Original opening screen with Tony and Sean](009-press-start/01-title.jpg)

![Start leads into the existing playable basement](009-press-start/02-gameplay.jpg)

### Changes and validation

- Enter/Space or controller A/Menu starts the game and preserves Tony's short briefing.
- M/controller Y toggles title sound; Q/controller B returns to the title from pause or job completion.
- Automated title lifecycle, keyboard/controller binding, tutorial, dialogue, gameplay, and sprite checks pass.
- Exported app visually checked in a small agent-test window; local code signature verifies.
- Normal launches remain maximized for Sean's playtests. Earlier chapters are preserved.

The illustrated giant toilet is title art, not an implemented boss. The sting is not a full soundtrack.
The mute setting lasts only for the current session. New title controller bindings have automated coverage;
physical-controller confirmation remains part of Sean's playtest. No source commit exists yet.
Original artwork was created with built-in imagegen; source and prompt are saved in `assets/title/`.
Markdown lint tooling remains unavailable locally; whitespace and line widths were checked directly.

## 010 — Choose your employee

**Date:** October 13, 2026 (America/Los_Angeles)

**Build:** Prototype 10 / 0.10.0 / Godot 4.7.2 / standalone macOS app

Tony and Sean are both playable. The confident fourth-generation plumber gets a fast pressure gun;
the idiot apprentice gets a heavy, slow plunger cannon. S.U.M.P., a CRT-faced robot company owner,
orders either employee into the basement. The working name means Supervisory Utility Management Processor.

### Changes and validation

- Press Start opens employee selection, with portraits, weapon stats, strengths, and weaknesses.
- Tony fires for 1 damage every 0.16 seconds; Sean fires for 3 damage every 0.60 seconds.
- Both retain the same forgiving movement and health. Restart and respawn preserve the employee choice.
- Tony has an original eight-pose sprite atlas; S.U.M.P. uses original code-drawn artwork.
- Title/selection, weapon cadence and damage, respawn, sprite alignment, and existing regression checks pass.
- The standalone macOS export succeeds and its local code signature verifies. No source commit exists yet.

The initial locked-Mac capture gap was resolved later on October 13. The exported build was checked in a small
agent-only window: selection, Tony's launch, S.U.M.P.'s briefing, gameplay, and return to title.
Physical-controller playtesting remains pending until Sean returns to the MacBook.

![Choose Tony or Sean under S.U.M.P.'s supervision](010-choose-your-employee/01-selection.jpg)

![S.U.M.P. briefs its employee](010-choose-your-employee/02-sump-briefing.jpg)

![Tony in the playable basement](010-choose-your-employee/03-tony-gameplay.jpg)

This is the first weapon-balance pass. S.U.M.P.'s name and design are provisional. There is no AI companion or co-op;
the unselected employee does not follow the player. Boss combat and the full mission remain future work.
Tony's sprite was made with built-in imagegen; the exact prompt is in `assets/sprites/tony-prompt-v1.json`.
Markdown lint tooling remains unavailable locally; document whitespace and line widths were checked directly.

It spans two lines to fit the card and emphasizes his expertise with a warmer tone.
