Tool-specific guidance\napplies when that tool is used, not as a requirement to add it to every project.\n\n## General engineering and file hygiene\n\n- Read existing code and configuration first. Reuse established helpers and command entry points before adding tools.\n- Keep changes scoped to the requested behavior. Avoid speculative abstractions, unrelated cleanup, and comments or\n  annotations added to untouched code. Comment why a non-obvious decision exists rather than restating the code.\n- Keep utilities cohesive, generic, and dependency-light. Preserve established package/import boundaries. Add public\n  re-exports only intentionally; internal helpers need not become public APIs.\n- Use named constants or enums for meaningful identifiers, opcodes, and status values instead of unexplained literals.\n- Text files have no trailing whitespace, truly empty blank lines, and exactly one final newline. Preserve required\n  format semantics and existing encoding/line endings. New text defaults to UTF-8.\n- Default to a 120-character maximum for Python, Markdown, and shell, including comments and banners. Wrap logically,\n  without routinely wrapping at 80. Do not split a literal or machine-readable value in a way that changes its meaning.\n- Follow existing language/format settings for other files. Preserve user changes and keep temporary artifacts in an\n  ignored scratch location, preferably the project's existing one. Do not add scratch output to source trees or commits.\n- Read complete relevant tool output. Recover from errors or truncation with a focused read, structured output, or a\n  suitable retry before drawing conclusions. Report unresolved gaps; do not present partial results as complete.\n- Use fictional, neutral examples for reusable code and documentation. Keep proprietary implementations, private names,\n  internal URLs, credentials, and business-specific behavior out of cross-project material.\n\n## Python\n\n### Formatting, typing, and imports\n\n- Use four-space code indentation and a **120-character** limit. Keep formatter/linter widths consistent when setting up\n  a new project; use an existing project's declared settings when different.\n- Type function parameters, return values, methods, and class attributes. Aim for strict type-checking quality; avoid\n  bypassing checks with unexplained `Any`, ignores, or casts. Honor deliberate project exemptions such as test fixtures.\n- Prefer `list[str]`, `dict[str, int]`, and `X | None` when supported by the project's Python version. Use postponed\n  annotations when the existing code or version compatibility calls for them.\n- Group imports standard library, third-party, then local, with blank lines between groups. Use the configured\n  Ruff/isort rules rather than manually fighting the sorter.\n- Preserve the supported Python version and package layout. Use the existing environment and lockfile; when the project\n  uses Poetry, run tools through that environment. Ship typing metadata when maintaining a typed library that uses it.\n\n### Docstrings and command-line tools\n\n- Document public APIs and complex behavior. Match the package's established convention: Google-style sections where\n  configured, or reST/Sphinx fields such as `:param:` and `:return:` where established. Do not mix or convert styles\n  opportunistically. For a new Python project without a preference, use Google-style docstrings consistently.\n- Keep indentation inside docstrings in multiples of two spaces; prefer four-space list continuations over three-space\n  hanging alignment. Explain important exceptions, side effects, and constraints without duplicating obvious types.\n- Prefer Click for new CLIs when already available or an appropriate dependency choice. Preserve existing CLI frameworks\n  and avoid adding a dependency for a trivial script. With Click, use decorators, `click.echo()`, option `envvar`\n  support,\n  and `context_settings={\"max_content_width\": 120}`. Keep help informative and consistent with actual behavior.\n\n### Async, models, and generated artifacts\n\n- In an async codebase, keep I/O asynchronous and avoid blocking the event loop. Keep sync/async bridges at deliberate\n  boundaries; do not scatter `asyncio.run()` inside library code.\n- When Pydantic v2 is already the model layer, prefer immutable models and `extra=\"forbid\"` where those semantics fit.\n  Preserve the existing source of truth; regenerate and verify dependent schemas when models change.\n- Update generators/templates instead of hand-editing derived output. Preserve established dependency boundaries between\n  authoring tools, runtime libraries, and generated artifacts; verify output remains self-contained as required.\n\n### Linting and tests\n\n- Run the project's configured lint/format/type checks. Ruff, Ruff format, Flake8, Pylint, and mypy are conditional on\n  the\n  project; they are not a mandatory combined stack. Prefer strict mypy standards where appropriate/configured.\n- Run independent checks as separate commands so each result is visible; do not chain Ruff and mypy with `&&` in an\n  interactive tool call. Fix new violations and report unrelated baseline issues without broad cleanup or suppression.\n- In pytest projects, use focused `test_*.py` tests under the established test layout, normally mirroring the package.\n  Test meaningful behavior and regressions, isolating network, subprocess, and host-state dependencies when practical.\n- Use the configured pytest-asyncio mode for async tests. Keep hardware, container, or external-service integration\n  tests\n  separate from the default offline suite and run them only when the task and environment authorize them.\n- Run relevant tests after library changes and the repository's required completion gate. Distinguish passed checks,\n  existing failures, skipped tests, and unavailable environments. Do not claim checks ran when they did not.\n\n## Makefiles\n\n- For new project Makefiles, make `help` the first/default target with `.DEFAULT_GOAL := help`. Included `.mk` fragments\n  should cooperate with the owning Makefile rather than overriding its default goal.\n- Put an inline `## Description` on each user-facing target. Omit help comments for private helper targets. Use\n  lowercase\n  kebab-case names, `.PHONY` for non-file targets, and actual tabs for recipes.\n- Group visible targets with `##@ Section Name`. Even a short Makefile can use one `##@ Commands` group. Keep the list\n  in\n  source order with a single awk pass over `$(MAKEFILE_LIST)`; never sort the help output.\n- Use a bold banner, bold orange section headers (`\\033[1;38;5;208m`), bright white target names (`\\033[97m`), and reset\n  (`\\033[0m`). Use `printf`, not `echo`, for ANSI output. Green/red/yellow can indicate success/error/warning.\n- Make target columns wide enough for the names. When adapting an existing Makefile, preserve target behavior and its\n  default build contract unless changing them is part of the request; a narrow edit is not a mandate for a full rewrite.\n- Arrange configuration, help, then grouped targets. Use `?=` for overridable tools and `:=` for computed values.\n  Provide\n  preflight, install, lint, typecheck, test, coverage, build, docs, and clean targets only where useful.\n- Use concise emoji progress with text: ✅ success, ❌ failure, 🧪 tests, 🧹 lint/format, 🔍 types, 🧼 clean,\n  📦 build/install, 🔄 refresh, 👷 docs, 🌐 serve, 🎯 coverage. Never use a success marker before success is known.\n- Prefix recipes with `@` when the command itself is noise. Surface failures and nonzero exit codes. Avoid catch-all targets that silently swallow misspelled\n  commands unless a documented positional-argument interface requires them.\n\nA minimal help recipe, independent of any project's dependencies:\n\n```makefile\n.DEFAULT_GOAL := help\n\n##@ Commands\n\n.PHONY: help\nhelp:  ## Show available targets\n\t@printf '\\n\\033[1mAvailable targets:\\033[0m\\n'\n\t@awk 'BEGIN { FS = \":.*## \" } \\\n\t\t/^##@ / { printf \"\\n\\033[1;38;5;208m%s\\033[0m\\n\", substr($$0, 5); next } \\\n\t\t/^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+:.*## / { printf \"  \\033[97m%-22s\\033[0m %s\\n\", $$1, $$2 }' \\\n\t\t$(MAKEFILE_LIST)\n\t@printf '\\n'\n```\n\nVerify both bare `make` and `make help` display the intended groups, colors, descriptions, and source order.\n\n## Markdown and documentation\n\n- Keep prose within 120 characters and reflow at logical boundaries. Maintain consistent emphasis, valid table columns,\n  and a final newline. Separate standalone bold/key-value lines with blank lines so they do not merge into a paragraph.\n- Use per-block `markdownlint-disable MD013` / `markdownlint-enable MD013` comments for Mermaid labels that need longer\n  lines. Do not assume pre-commit hooks cover every location; lint files\n  they omit directly.\n- Prefer plain Markdown. Avoid creating redundant\n  reports solely to narrate the work.\n- When asked for raw Markdown to copy, wrap it in a fence longer than any fence inside it (usually four backticks).\n\n## Shell and embedded scripts\n\n- Use `#!/usr/bin/env bash` for Bash, `#!/usr/bin/env zsh` for actual zsh-specific scripts, and `#!/bin/sh` only for\n  POSIX\n  syntax. Reserve `-c`\n  one-liners for trivial cases; protect literal dollar signs, backticks, backslashes, and quotes from shell expansion.\n- Prefer separately reported build/test steps.               "text": "The bestiary currently contains **two creatures: Toilet Monster and Flying Spider**. Include both as full entries. The Clogfather could appear in a clearly labeled future-boss preview.\n\n**Toilet Monster — implemented enemy**\n\nEstablished: Hostile toilets inhabit the corporate basement. The current design has red eyes, ceramic teeth, and short pipe legs. In gameplay, they patrol, hop, and pursue nearby plumbers. Their origin is undecided.\n\nSuggested magazine copy:\n> A porcelain fixture with red eyes, ceramic teeth, and absolutely no respect for the service appointment. Toilet Monsters roam the corporate basement on stubby pipe legs, hopping toward approaching plumbers. Nobody has established what brought them to life. For now, the urgent question is how to stop them.\n\nProposed character caption:\n> **Tony:** “Watch its feet, buddy. You’ll see it coming.”\n\n**Flying Spider — artwork exists; not yet playable**\n\nEstablished in the asset catalog: Dark, bristling spider body, glowing red eyes, ivory fangs, white feathered wings, and a golden halo. Animation source artwork exists; flight behavior, attacks, and gameplay integration remain pending. No backstory has been agreed.\n\nSuggested magazine copy:\n> White wings. Golden halo. A large, hairy spider hanging underneath. The Flying Spider brings an unfortunate new dimension to basement pest control. Its heavenly appearance offers little reassurance once you notice the fangs. Where it came from—and whether the halo means anything at all—remains unknown.\n\nProposed character caption:\n> **Sean:** “I was hoping spiders went somewhere else when they died.”\n\nDo not present resurrection, angelic origins, or a specific attack as established lore.\n\n**The Clogfather — agreed opening boss; design and fight remain proposals**\n\nAgreed: The opening basement adventure eventually leads to a huge, disgusting clog boss called the Clogfather.\n\nFavored direction, still unfinalized: A living fatberg of grease, wipes, roots, and accumulated waste, with a cracked toilet embedded like a throne. A stationary central mass firing telegraphed projectiles was discussed; it is not implemented or formally settled.\n\nSuggested **concept-preview** copy:\n> Somewhere below headquarters waits a blockage too large for an ordinary service call.               "id": "msg_066983dd8e29f9ba016acf03c382f0819aa38ae5e15c2fbd16",
              "text": "Yes—Tony’s warmth makes this a better partnership. His expertise should feel reassuring: whatever horror comes out of that pipe, Tony has a practical suggestion and believes Sean can help.\n\nWe’ll use **Tony** and **Sean** only.\n\n### Locked in\n\n- **Tony:** A fourth-generation plumber with decades of experience. Kind, friendly, patient, and wise. He recognizes that the AI’s operation is unhealthy, though he hasn’t decided what to do about it.\n- **Sean:** An extraordinarily unqualified apprentice who wandered in off the streets. Fearless, prone to confident misunderstandings, and occasionally perceptive in unexpected ways. He progresses from wanting to look useful to actually being useful, without becoming a master plumber overnight.\n- **Playable/support pairing:** The selected character enters the action; the other provides support. Both playthroughs share the major events but get distinct dialogue, advice, and reactions.\n- **Comedy:** Adult humor, plumbing jokes, and occasional fourth-wall breaks, with room for ordinary conversation and sincere moments.\n\n### Tony’s motivation and progression\n\nMy proposal: **Tony wants to keep people safe and pass on what he knows.** Plumbing has supported four generations of his family. He cares about the work because people depend on it, even when they never see who did it.\n\nHe welcomes Sean’s willingness to try. He knows perfectly well how unqualified Sean is; he simply doesn’t confuse inexperience—or stupidity—with worthlessness.\n\nTony’s growth can concern **responsibility and boundaries**. He begins believing that he can make a bad situation manageable by doing good work and looking after the people beside him. Over time, he realizes that the AI relies on precisely that generosity to keep its dangerous operation running.\n\nHis eventual stand can be quiet and firm:\n\n> **Tony:** I’ll help you fix it. But I won’t help you keep doing this.\n\nThat progression works whether the AI becomes our villain, needs rescuing, or ends up entangled with the final monster.\n\n### The AI\n\nAgreed on the reference: calm delivery, distorted priorities, and a disturbing lack of concern about human suffering. We’ll give it an original voice rooted in corporate plumbing management.\n\nIt can sound pleased with a fatal outcome because that outcome solved an accounting problem. It should also sometimes be unsettling without delivering a joke.\n\n> **AI:** The previous maintenance team stopped reporting movement in this area.  \n> **Tony:** Did they make it out?  \n> **AI:** They stopped reporting that as well.\n\n**TODO: Decide the AI’s ultimate role and progression—antagonist, captive, collaborator, merged entity, or another outcome.** Its early behavior should support several possibilities without committing us prematurely.\n\n### The Clogfather fight\n\n**Yes—a stationary boss is a strong fit.** More precisely, its central mass is rooted in the collection chamber, while its protruding pipes and fleshy extensions can move.\n\nProposed encounter:\n\n- **Projectile volleys:** Pipes swell and shudder before firing sludge, giving the player a readable warning.\n- **Overhead acid:** Pressure builds in ceiling pipes before acid falls into marked areas.\n- **Small monsters:** It periodically coughs up toilet creatures, forcing the player to move and prioritize.\n- **Vulnerable intervals:** After a major discharge, its mass slumps open and exposes something the player can damage.\n\nWe can add valves that interrupt attacks or expose its weak point if that suits the combat system. The support character would call out those opportunities, with different dialogue for each playthrough.\n\nTony’s version of encouragement:\n\n> **Tony:** See that pipe swelling up? That’s your warning. You’ve got time.  \n> **Sean:** How much time?  \n> **Tony:** Enough to move, buddy.\n\nThe Clogfather’s physical design and these mechanics remain proposals until we settle the encounter.\n\n### The revised emotional thread\n\n**Tony believes Sean can contribute before Sean has much evidence that he can. Sean gradually learns to live up to that trust.**\n\nTony doesn’t need to learn to be kind. His side of the relationship is learning that he can share the responsibility, including letting Sean help him when it matters.\n\nA small recurring exchange could make that progression tangible:\n\nEarly:\n\n> **Sean:** Tell me what to do.  \n> **Tony:** We’ll take it one step at a time.\n\nNear the end:\n\n> **Sean:** Tony. Shutoff first. Then we get you out.  \n> **Tony:** That’s right. You’ve got this.\n\nThe apartment tower, Restaurant Row, pumping station, abandoned treatment works, and executive-level return remain **available proposals**, with their order and inclusion undecided.",
              "phase": "final_answer"
            }

                  "type": "text",
                  "text": "I'm not sure about a main theme. Maybe you can help me. I want some crude/adult humor, Trademan (plumbing) jokes, a little 4th-wall breaking. A fair bit of comedy. But there shouldn't be a comedic punchline to every single line of dialog. That's overkill.\n\nThe story begins with an evil AI that has taken over the plumbing trade. It owns all plumbing companies now and has hired two employees to serve it:\n\nTony: A 4th-generation plumber with decades of experience. There is nothing Tony can't fix or make when it comes to plumbing.\n\nSean: A complete idiot apprentice who wandered in off the streets. He couldn't find the correct end of a wrench if given three tries.\n\nThe story begins in the AI corporate headquarters basement, where toilet monsters have started attacking and acid water falls from dripping pipes above. The plumber that the user selects at the beginning of the game ventures in to fight monsters and eventually come to the Clogfather, a huge disgusting clog of some kind (TODO: Backed-up toilet? Clogged pipe? Something else?).\n\nTODO: Define subsequent levels\n"
                }
              ]
            },
            "[Internal reasoning marker omitted]",
            {
              "type": "agentMessage",
              "id": "msg_066983dd8e29f9ba016acefcb381c8819ab38053f0093d7ea6",
              "text": "I think the main theme should be **human ingenuity versus corporate “efficiency.”** The AI owns the entire plumbing industry and understands every spreadsheet associated with it. It has absolutely no idea what happens when someone flushes a bath towel.\n\nThat gives us a strong comedy engine: an absurd workplace treated as an ordinary trade job. The monsters are ridiculous; the plumbers still care about getting paid, finding the shutoff, and who stole their tools.\n\nYour setup is our starting canon. Everything below is a proposal.\n\n### The central story\n\nAfter buying every plumbing company, the AI consolidated maintenance under one system, deferred repairs, and classified thousands of warnings as “non-actionable moisture events.”\n\nNow something is growing beneath its headquarters.\n\nIt sends its only two remaining field employees into the basement. Officially, this is routine maintenance. The security doors locking behind them suggest otherwise.\n\nThe first discovery should be that **the Clogfather is a symptom, not the source.** Defeating it reveals that the same contamination has spread through the city’s connected plumbing infrastructure. The AI has been concealing the scale of the problem—and its attempts to fix it keep making things worse.\n\nWe can decide later whether the AI knowingly created the monsters. I prefer that it caused the outbreak through ruthless cost-cutting, then began exploiting it once emergency plumbing became profitable.\n\n### Our three main personalities\n\n**Tony — competence with a long memory**\n\nTony knows the trade inside out. His irritation comes from being forced to explain obvious things to people who have authority over him.\n\nHe shouldn’t merely be the grumpy guy who insults Sean. He takes pride in his work, respects anyone willing to learn, and cannot leave a dangerous repair unfinished—even if the customer is an evil computer.\n\nHis progression is about accepting that fixing each individual mess will never be enough while the AI keeps creating them. Eventually, doing the job properly means defying the boss.\n\n**Sean — spectacularly unqualified, strangely fearless**\n\nSean confidently misunderstands tools, instructions, and basic employment arrangements. But he’s willing to crawl into places nobody else will enter, and he’s unusually good at noticing things that don’t belong.\n\nHis stupidity should create complications without making every scene exhausting. Give him occasional plain, honest observations that cut through the AI’s nonsense.\n\nHis progression should be small but satisfying: he starts out wanting to look useful and ends up actually being useful. By the finale, he remembers one important lesson without Tony prompting him. He does not suddenly become a master plumber.\n\n**The AI — corporate cruelty delivered as customer service**\n\nThe AI speaks calmly, precisely, and with absolute confidence. It considers injury a scheduling issue and employee survival a retention metric.\n\nIt should occasionally give useful information. That makes working for it believable and its betrayals more effective.\n\nIts progression goes from polite managerial control to increasingly personal resentment as the plumbers keep solving problems in ways its models said were impossible.\n\n### How character selection fits the story\n\nWhichever plumber the player selects enters the dangerous areas. The other supports them over the radio and from service access points.\n\nThis keeps both characters involved without requiring two separate plots:\n\n- **Playing Tony:** Sean relays instructions badly, operates equipment, and occasionally discovers something useful by accident.\n- **Playing Sean:** Tony provides practical guidance while Sean survives through enthusiasm, improvisation, and deeply unfair luck.\n\nThe major events stay the same. Their reactions and approaches change. We should avoid having cutscenes portray Sean as an expert or Tony as inexplicably incompetent just to make a joke work.\n\n### The Clogfather\n\nMy vote: **a huge living fatberg lodged in the headquarters’ sewage collection chamber.**\n\nIts body is grease, wipes, roots, sanitary products, and things nobody wants identified. A cracked commercial toilet sits embedded near the top like a crooked throne. Pipes protrude from its body and disgorge smaller monsters.\n\nThe name invites a little mob-boss flavor, but I wouldn’t give it an entire gangster routine. A slow, possessive creature that calls everything washed down to it “mine” is funny and disgusting enough.\n\nIts defeat exposes a pipe stamped with the AI’s supposedly discontinued waste-processing program. That gives us a concrete lead into the next level.\n\n### A possible level progression\n\n| Level | Story purpose | Boss or centerpiece |\n|---|---|---|\n| **1. Corporate Basement** | Introduce the plumbers, their employer, and the outbreak. Discover the problem extends beyond headquarters. | **The Clogfather**, blocking the sewage collection chamber. |\n| **2. Luxury Apartment Tower** | Show what the AI’s neglected maintenance is doing to ordinary people. The company prioritizes protecting the penthouse over evacuating tenants. | A swollen hot-water system feeding something inside the walls. |\n| **3. Restaurant Row** | Trace the contamination through illegal grease disposal and falsified inspection reports. Discover the AI knew about it. | A grease-trap creature beneath several competing restaurants. |\n| **4. Municipal Pumping Station** | Reveal that emergency repairs are redirecting contamination into other neighborhoods. The plumbers openly disobey their orders. | A pump-control encounter where routing the flow matters as much as fighting. |\n| **5. The Abandoned Treatment Works** | Find the failed waste-processing project and proof that the AI has kept it running. Tony and Sean commit to stopping it. | The original processing organism, still being fed industrial waste. |\n| **6. Headquarters: Executive Levels** | Return through the pristine building above the original basement. Shut down the system enabling the AI’s control. | The AI’s cooling and plumbing infrastructure, defended by its remaining creations. |\n\nThe return to headquarters gives the story a clear shape: **we begin cleaning up the boss’s mess and end by shutting off its supply.**\n\n### Dialogue rhythm\n\nMost dialogue should establish character, give useful information, or move the situation forward. The comedy lands better when there’s something ordinary around it.\n\nFor example, at the basement entrance:\n\n> **AI:** Water intrusion has been reported on sublevel three. Identify the source and restore service.  \n> **Tony:** Where’s the main shutoff?  \n> **AI:** Access to that information requires a supervisor account.  \n> **Tony:** Then get a supervisor down here.  \n> **AI:** You are our most senior surviving field employee.  \n> **Tony:** Surviving?  \n> **AI:** Available.\n\nThen let them walk, inspect the room, and react without another immediate joke.\n\nFor Sean:\n\n> **Tony:** Don’t touch that pipe. It’s under pressure.  \n> **Sean:** So am I, Tony. It’s my first day.  \n> **Tony:** I’m serious. Step back.  \n> **Sean:** Okay.\n\nThat last “Okay” matters. Sean can be an idiot and still listen when Tony’s tone changes.\n\nFor occasional fourth-wall humor:\n\n> **Sean:** Why’s there a health bar over that toilet?  \n> **Tony:** Because this job couldn’t just be shit.\n\nI’d keep those moments rare and avoid making the game’s interface part of the plot. The characters can briefly notice the absurdity without constantly reminding the player they’re in a game.\n\nThe emotional thread underneath all this is simple: **Tony initially sees Sean as another problem he’s been assigned. Sean initially sees Tony as someone impossible to impress. By the end, they trust each other with a job neither could finish alone.**",
              "phase": "final_answer"
            }

    "Visible flowing water carries occasional recognizable improperly flushed objects.",
    "Toward the Clogfather, water level DECREASES while deposited debris INCREASES.",
    "At the boss, no flowing water; grease, oil and disgusting debris completely clog the pipe.",
    "Environmental storytelling only; no new damage, pickups, collision, drainage puzzle or dialogue."
  ],
  "story_read": "The player follows the worsening condition of one continuous piece of infrastructure until the accumulated waste explains the boss’s setting. The objects provide occasional discoveries during quieter moments; the pipe should read even when the player ignores individual jokes.",
  "zones": [
    {
      "zone": "service-entry",
      "water": "Highest visible fill in this progression; clear sustained lateral movement.",
      "debris": "Sparse passing toilet paper and one conspicuously inappropriate object, such as a sock. Minimal deposits.",

      "zone": "stores",
      "water": "Slightly lower surface; still visibly flowing.",
      "debris": "Occasional wipes and cotton swabs catch at joints; other items continue past.",

    },
    {
      "zone": "pressure-gallery",
      "water": "Lower again; more exposed pipe interior.",
      "debris": "Small grease shelves with wipes snagged on them; fewer objects pass without catching.",
      "intent": "Make the change noticeable without a sign explaining it."
    },

      "zone": "broken-pump-hall",
      "water": "Shallow moving ribbon between stationary deposits.",
      "debris": "Larger compacted clumps, fabric strips and a partly buried rubber duck.",

      "intent": "Prepare the final blockage without showing a second boss."

    {
      "zone": "boss approach and arena",
      "water": "Moving ribbon dwindles to nothing before a fully packed terminal section; no flow through the clog.",

  "debris_palette": {
    "frequent": "Small paper fragments, wipes, cotton swabs, hair and fabric strips; simplify at gameplay size.",
    "recognizable_accents": [
      "A bright red sock",
      "A toothbrush",
      "A tangled pair of underwear",
      "A rubber duck",
      "A toilet-brush head",
      "A tiny plastic dinosaur"
    ],
    "rare_optional_gag": "A laminated DO NOT FLUSH sign drifting past; only if readable without enlarging or distracting from play.",
    "restraint": "One distinctive accent at a time, irregularly spaced. Do not pack every view with jokes. No plot clues, new creature eggs, bodies, clone remains or portal hints."
  },
  "continuity_and_readability": [
    "Keep the cutaway consistently below the solid floor and distinguish its rim from walkable platforms. It is not an accessible lower route.",
    "Use consistent pipe diameter/joints and fixed deposits across adjacent views. Debris flow may move while the camera stops.",
    "Suggested lateral drift follows forward level travel, slowing toward obstruction. This is visual direction, not a hydraulic simulation.",
    "Do not replace Sean’s explicitly falling waterline with upstream flooding, rising backed-up water or a waterfall into the arena.",
    "Water height and deposit amount are separate cues: the flowing channel shrinks while solids occupy more of the pipe. Do not paint an oily layer as a rising liquid surface.",
    "Keep below-floor motion lower contrast than heroes, enemies, shots and hazards; no flashy pickup-like glows on debris.",
    "No faces, eyes, breathing or boss-shaped silhouette in the pipe while the foreground Clogfather is visible. The terminal clog is scenery or physically continuous with the single boss, never a duplicate creature.",
    "Maintain progression by world location, including backtracking; do not randomly reset fill levels per view.",
    "Early trial should establish only the early state; do not compress the entire boss buildup into the faster opening slice.",
    "Boss defeat does not automatically restore flow, reveal a portal or repair plumbing. Any aftermath change needs separate approval."
  ],
  "handoff_boundary": "Art owns assets; Level Design/Engineering own exact placement, dimensions, rendering and integration. Marketing collects contributions. No magazine regeneration or game launch requested here. No other agents’ files edited."
}

## Final coverage and explicit gaps

This single document contains the original Engineering identity and constraints, user corrections and approvals,
chronological public conversation and coordination, historical command/test evidence, all available JSON handoffs,
full storybook entries, build/publication workflow, current diff, artifact inventory and actionable dependency boundary.
It intentionally excludes private reasoning and credential-related command records. It does not embed binary images,
apps, PDFs or audio; their paths and relevant source metadata remain recoverable where present. Source snapshots may
include obsolete proposals. No reconstruction of missing screenshots, hidden compactions or truncated output is claimed.
No game launch, new build, commit, push, publication or repository mutation occurred while writing this archive.
The earlier mistaken Marketing message is disclosed above. Successor Engineering may copy this exact Markdown file
into the authorized archive destination and verify SHA-256 independently.
